subsubtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-DISCRIMINATION AGAINST LOW-PAID EMPLOYEES-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In light of the decision of the Canadian Human Rights Commission that the federal government is discriminating against 3,000 low-paid, mainly female, public servants; the commission has decided that employees in the female-dominated food services, laundry services and related services are paid substantially less than the male-dominated stores and warehouse occupations; in view of the commission's ruling that the jobs are considered equal in value; and since the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) ignores this shocking disparity, despite repeated representations for equal pay, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald):
That as a matter of good faith, the President of the Treasury Board move immediately to rectify this gross inequity in the public service, the result of which is to further discriminate against women, and that his action include compensation for one year's back wages.

speechtext:

there is little the federal government can do about the serious effects of the drought situation on the prairies, but that the government must look as if it is doing something by publicity stunts, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom):

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question would be for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, but in his absence I will direct it to the Prime Minister.

subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext: He is looking for help. Answer it yourself, Pierre.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext:
The Prime Minister will recall that on May 4, 1979, an agreement was initialled between Canada and Mexico, one sentence of which reads as follows:
The government of Mexico undertakes to supply and the Government of Canada assures the purchase of up to 100,000 barrels per day of crude oil during the validity of the present agreement and in conformity with the program referred to in this article.
In 1979 it was 100,000 barrels per day, but today an agreement was signed by which Mexico will be sending Canada only 50,000 barrels per day. Will the Prime Minister tell the House what happened to that lost 50,000 barrels of oil per day?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if the right hon. Leader of the Opposition compares the two agreements, he is right: he will see that the figure
100.000	no longer appears. In that respect, we feel the agreement reached today is not as satisfactory as the one that had been initialled last year.

subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext: Just how?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext:
On the other hand, there is an improvement in the terms of the other half of the agreement, that concerning
50.000	barrels per day. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition will recall that last year the undertaking of the Mexicans was to go up to 50,000 barrels of oil per day. Now the agreement is specific as not being "up to" but, in fact, 50,000 barrels per day.
He will also see that the agreement last year was to reach that figure of up to 50,000 some time in the 12 months following 1980, whereas the terms of this agreement make that delivery of 50,000 barrels effective this December; therefore, a year in advance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Madam Speaker. I would call the attention of the Prime Minister to the language

May 27, 1980
Oral Questions
of the agreement initialled last year. It does not suggest, "up to
50.000	barrels per day"; it says, "shall reach 50,000 barrels per day". That clearly indicates that the 50,000 barrels would be achieved by the agreement that was initialled and apparently abandoned.
The Prime Minister has said that somehow or other Canada benefits from having lost 50,000 barrels per day of imported oil from Mexico. Will he tell the House how we benefit from having lost, in the course of a year, 50,000 barrels per day from Mexico?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am afraid the Leader of the Opposition does not understand correctly the agreement initialled last year. It was a "best efforts" by the Mexicans toward 100,000; it was not a certain undertaking of reaching
100,000.	That part of the agreement, I admit to the Leader of the Opposition, does not appear this year. There is still a "best efforts" clause, but not linked with specific figures. I can only repeat to the House what I have just said: we have not that
100.000	figure, but we have gained 12 months in the deliverance of the 50,000 figure.

subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext: You have lost 50,000 barrels.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the "best efforts" in the agreement that was initialled last year referred to the 100,000 barrels per day. It was in relation to that that the phrase "best efforts" occurred. There was a clear commitment of up to
50.000	barrels a day: "shall reach". There was a clear commitment that the exports "shall reach" 50,000 barrels a day in the agreement that was initialled in May of last year. What has happened is that this government, in the course of twelve months, has lost 50,000 barrels of oil a day for Canada from Mexico.

subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext: Fumbling and bumbling.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext: The figures last year in the initialled agreement were spelled out in the agreement. There are no figures spelled out in the agreement that was signed today.

subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext: Right on.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext: You blew it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext:
The figures are included in a joint statement by the President and the Prime Minister, but they are not part of a formal agreement signed on behalf of the two governments. Can the Prime Minister give us a clear assurance that the
50.000	barrels a day-down 50,000 from what Canadians had a right to expect-is a firm figure and will not change, as the
100.000	barrels a day of last May changed in a year?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext: You blew it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext:
The reason it does not appear in the agreement, Madam Speaker, is that it appears in a specific contract
of understanding between Pemex, the Mexican petroleum company, and Petro-Canada. If the hon. Leader of the Opposition cares to refer to that, there is a specific agreement between the exporter and the importer that the figure of
50,000	will be reached, I repeat, this December rather than December, 1981.
All 1 can say, Madam Speaker, is that indeed it would have been preferable if the additional figure of 100,000 "best efforts" had appeared. It does not. The Mexicans did change their minds on that.
I would hope that the agreement that our government negotiated last May, and which was initialled by the two parties, had been followed up rapidly by the then Government of Canada and that the visit of the President of Mexico had indeed taken place within months of that signature, which was our intention had we remained the government. The party opposite then formed the government and postponed that visit for a full year, which gave the Mexicans time to change their minds.

subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED

Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister knows full well that that is not the case. But the fact remains that he has admitted that there is now a loss of 50,000 barrels a day- between May of last year and May of this year. He admits that.
Will he tell us what went wrong? Will he tell us what actions by the Government of Canada caused the Mexicans to back away from their "best efforts" commitment toward 100,000 barrels a day and to settle for only 50,000 barrels a day? What accounts for the lost 50,000 barrels a day?

subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED

speechtext: Hear, hear!

May 27, 1980

subtopic: CANADA-MEXICO OIL AGREEMENT-NUMBER OF BARRELS TO BE IMPORTED
speechtext:
My question to the Prime Minister is this: The government has lost 50,000 barrels of oil from Mexico. Imports from Venezuela will be down from 240,000 barrels in the first quarter to 150,000 barrels in the last quarter of this year. Madam Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I hesitate to bring forward the perennial point of privilege about a situation that members on all sides sometimes experience but, quite frankly, Your Honour, my patience has almost come to the end. Any sensitivity for the issues before this country would have perhaps given some direction to the Chair as to why I have been rising right from the beginning of the question period for two days, having asked three to four questions in English and one question in French during the total time of this session. I do not rise frivolously in most cases, and I have not asked a frivolous question this session.
I have a matter that could potentially grievously affect my province in Atlantic Canada, and particularly my riding. There have been three members on this side of the House recognized today, fellow colleagues, admittedly, who were also recognized by Your Honour yesterday. The hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), for whom I have great fondness

May 27, 1980
Privilege-Mr. Nowlart
and affection, was not on any list on Monday and was not on any list today, but you recognized him twice and still have been able to have a blind eye for this seat.
I would like to know what system the Chair uses. Admittedly you recognize front benchers, and you have help to guide the Chair, with which I fully agree; but I felt that once the question period was open the priority related to when members commenced to rise. I do not mind getting my exercise, Madam Speaker. I certainly enjoy getting exercise. But at some time I would like to know why my rising does not take precedence over other hon. members.
That is my question of privilege, Your Honour. I do not think either of the two ministers involved in the questions I wish to ask are going to be here tomorrow and I have given notice to both of them.

speechtext:
Order, please. I have already explained to the House what is my policy in conducting the question period. I did say that, of course, when front benchers want to get into the question period and I know they might have a supplementary to a question asked by another member, I allow them to ask those supplementary questions because I want the question period to be as lively as possible and to bring out as much information as possible.
As for the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan), his name was on the list of those who have risen in the House for several days. I do acknowledge that. I recognize hon. members in the order in which they have risen and the hon. member's name was the fifth to come up on my list, but we did not get to him before three o'clock.
Many members rise and I try to recognize them in the order in which they do so. I am assisted in that regard, to be as fair as possible, by the Clerk who tries to give me that order. 1 do my best in trying to recognize members as soon and as often as possible, but it is not possible to recognize everyone every day. On subsequent days I bring back the names on my list, but if hon. members are not in the House it is quite obvious I cannot recognize them. I cannot keep them on the list for five or six days in a row. That is my policy and the system that I have tried to establish in order to satisfy all members, but we all know that is impossible.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 hope to be able to convince Your Honour that I have a question of privilege in relation to a matter which affects most hon. members of this Parliament and, indeed, many of the members of the Thirty-first Parliament. It is a matter that has just come to my attention through an inquiry made to the office of the Clerk of this House. The problem is that a custom, nay a tradition, of Parliament may be destroyed by a simple administrative decision.
The Thirty-first Parliament was unique to many people for many reasons. For example, for some it was their only stint as a member of Parliament. It may or may not have been the shortest Parliament on record; the record will show whether it was or was not. It was unquestionably the first Progressive Conservative administration for 16 years. I am confident that it will prove to have been the first, but not the last, of which the right hon. member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) was prime minister. It may be the only one during which the right hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Trudeau) was leader of the official opposition, as they tell me he is going to retire again.
Members of the House and, indeed, visitors to the Parliament buildings stroll through the corridors here and view various contributions to the history of this country. I am informed reliably now that composite photographs of the members of the Thirty-first Parliament of Canada will not be produced.

subtopic: RESIGNATION OF HON. LINCOLN M. ALEXANDER
RESIGNATION OF HON. LINCOLN M. ALEXANDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I hope that you will forgive me if I take a few moments of the time of this House. 1 know that there are matters of significant importance which must be debated, but I feel that it is necessary, after having spent 12 years in this House, to give some credibility to what is already a fact, that I will be leaving my "family", as I would like to have it known, this House of Commons, because I have accepted a position with the Workmen's Compensation Board of Ontario.
I wish you well, Madam Speaker. 1 saw that you were being tested today. I think that you have the fortitude and excellence of mind to handle yourself in your new position. I am sorry that 1 did not have an opportunity to become more involved and to challenge you as well, but I thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak to the House.
I have been touched by the excitement of this place. I have been moved by the challenges and touched by the joys and disappointments. But what is more important to me is that I have been touched by the friendships which I know I have made, because I have received so many letters wishing me well. When my friend from Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) triggered that spontaneous standing ovation, it was a good thing that I did not have to speak at that time because there were tears in my eyes. I am not ashamed to say that I was not able to control myself. That was a great tribute and one 1 will never forget.
That is why I feel so sad at this particular time. This is a great family and a tremendous institution. When I think of the
Resignation of Member
criticism which comes from all quarters, I say to my colleagues, "Forget it, because you are serving". Let those who criticize try to get into this place. There are so many who try to get in, but who cannot make it.
However, I have been blessed. I am grateful to three of four people, who I would like to single out, with your patience, Madam Speaker. The late Right Hon. John George Diefen-baker is the one who asked me to run, who believed that I should be here in this House and who believed that I had a role to play. No matter where he may be, I hope that I have not disappointed him.
I remember Bob Stanfield. He plucked me from what is called the back benches and honoured me by making me a critic in the shadow cabinet.
Of course, there is the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) who made me a cabinet minister. Madam Speaker and my dear colleagues, I stand here naked because in my wildest dreams I never believed that I would represent my country as a member of Parliament or that it was possible I would represent my country as a cabinet minister.
Yes, I will have some very fond memories of this place, but 1 think it must be recognized that there are many around us who make our lives more successful. It is not only the "me's" and the "I's" who are fortunate to be sitting here temporarily, but I think of those who are involved in Hansard, the maintenance department, the office of the Clerk, the Sergeant-at-Arms, security, the post office, public servants and even the media- although, there are a couple I would like to mention specifically, but I will let them know that I have love and forgiveness in my heart! Frankly, I could not care less what they think about me anyway.
I care about what the hon. members of this House think of me, and I care about what the people of Hamilton West think of me. 1 am pleased to have concrete evidence that they thought enough of me to send me back to this House on five occasions. But to those people to whom I made reference, I would like to say thank you, because without their assistance and help the Alexanders and anyone else you would like to mention, Madam Speaker, would not be effective in this House of Commons. They are the people who protect us and who look after us. I would like publicly to thank them now for looking after me for the past 12 years.

subtopic: RESIGNATION OF HON. LINCOLN M. ALEXANDER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: RESIGNATION OF HON. LINCOLN M. ALEXANDER
speechtext:
These people have made my task very easy and very pleasant. I would like to extend a special thanks to Labour Canada. Although I was not there long, they did keep me out of trouble, and I thank them from the bottom of my heart. I wish them well because they are a fine group of people. When a new government takes charge and new ministers are appointed, there are some who believe that perhaps the public servants are not on their side. I can stand here and say that I had the confidence of my department, for which I am very grateful and I thank them.

May 27, 1980
Tributes to Mr. Alexander
Last but not least, I want to thank the constituents of Hamilton West who gave me their confidence, loyalty, and faith over the years. It is in this area that I feel a little confused and a little sad because they were counting on me. However, I will not disappoint them in the future because I am going into another area of service. I can advise them, as I can advise my colleagues here, that you expect much of me, that you want me to do a good job and I will not disappoint you, as I have tried not to disappoint you in all the years I have been here.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I would like to tell you in all sincerity and from the bottom of my heart that I will miss this place. But I think having served in this place I am a much better person, and for that I am grateful. Thank you very much.
[Editor's note: Mr. Alexander received a standing ovation.]

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would now indicate to you that I resign my seat in the House of Commons for the constituency of Hamilton West effective midnight, May 28, 1980.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think this is one occasion on which 1 can truly claim to speak on behalf of all members of the House of Commons when I say to the member of Parliament for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) just how very much he will be missed in this assembly, in the work of Parliament and of government. I think it is true to say that no member of Parliament is better liked in this House and that no member of Parliament will be more sorely missed by his colleagues.
The hon. member for Hamilton West served here with distinction for 12 productive years. He became a symbol of Canadian democracy and a spokesman for Canadians in need across this land. He served his constituency with care and sensitivity. He served in cabinet as an outstanding minister of labour. But more importantly to him and to us, he won the respect and affection of all who were associated with the House of Commons.
We all wish him well in the new responsibilities which he has accepted, but this House of Commons will miss Lincoln Alexander and will long remember him as one of the outstanding individuals ever to have served in this Parliament.

Madam Speaker, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) was perfectly correct when he said that on this occasion he was speaking for everyone in this House of Commons. I should just like to make that very clear and very certain by associating the New Democratic Party with the sentiments that have been expressed.
I rise to speak on behalf of my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), who, like the hon. member for
Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), first came here in 1968. I also speak on behalf of all my colleagues.
We enjoyed the remarks the hon. member made today in his final speech in this chamber. I think what appealed to us most-at least, it appealed to me-was his emphasis on the friendships he has developed in this assembly, friendships that he will carry with him through the rest of his life. We have not always agreed with the hon. member. He and I have had some interesting discussions, but more often than not we have agreed and we have common interests. He has served this place with distinction. He has put forth his best effort and he fully deserves the tributes we have been paying to him in these few moments today.
We say goodbye to Lincoln Alexander from the House of Commons and we wish him the very best through all the years that lie ahead.

We both went to Osgoode Hall law school and got to know each other very well over the years. Of course, he has been much more successful than I, and I guess he was more successful in law school as well. He has certainly been more successful politically. Although we were both elected in 1968, I sort of took a sabbatical from 1972 to 1974 while he continued to serve here. We have both been around since that time, Madam Speaker.

I have enjoyed working with the hon. member these many years. He is going on to his reward with a new career-a career with the Workmen's Compensation Board in the province of Ontario. Thank you, Madam Speaker, for permitting me this opportunity of adding my voice to those of the leader of the Conservative party and others in paying tribute to one who is best described as a very personal friend.
When the hon. gentleman arrived in this House in 1968, I was then the minister of labour. In a comparatively short period of time I was very much aware of a rather brash, talented new member of the opposition party. In no time at all, as I recall, the hon. member became the Official Opposition critic of the labour portfolio. One day I called him over after a rather tough question or two and expressed the opinion that he
May 27, 1980

had perhaps been a little unfair. He reminded me that he had patterned his particular style after mine, which made it very difficult for me. He is a very charming individual.
I repeat what has often been said, that this is a very unique institution. I recall the hon. member and his wife coming with us to the ILO convention in Geneva in the early seventies. 1 had an opportunity to break bread with him and get to know him well. I must admit that 1 have always had a particularly soft spot for the hon. gentleman, particularly since he is the member of Parliament for the riding in which my mother lives.
I am not just sure how she voted in the last election, since very early in the campaign she received a personal visit from the hon. member.
In conclusion, I want to say as one who left this House in 1976 that it is not at best a very easy decision. If we are selfish we tend to remain here because we enjoy the company of members, the challenge and the unpredictability of the House of Commons if you are a House of Commons man.
I recall on a similar occasion that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) expressed the wish that perhaps one day fortune would be such that I would be back in the House of Commons. I hope that what happened to me does not happen to the hon. gentleman.
I know, from the hon. member's record in this House of Commons and particularly from his compassion when he was minister of labour for those wonderful Canadians who do manual work for a living, that he is more than adequate to fulfil the role of head of Ontario's workmen's compensation board. I bridled and went to the defence of the hon. member when, shortly after his appointment, it was suggested by certain members of the press that he lacked the qualifications for the job. I think, Madam Speaker, that the qualities which the hon. gentleman has exemplified so many times here- compassion, concern, curiosity, willingness and devotion to work-are all the qualifications he needs to fill this very sensitive position, and I wish him well.

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, May 26, consideration of the motion of Mrs. Begin that Bill C-16, to amend the Old Age Security Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN MAXIMUM MONTHLY AMOUNT OF SUPPLEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not so certain that the continuation of this debate at this time is appropriate following on the heels of the announcement by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) that he is retiring from the House of Commons. As we are all aware, it is not his intention to retire from active life and he will continue to serve his country in another function for many more years to come.
May 27, 1980

1 have been listening with great interest to the debate on Bill C-16 as it has continued, and I must say that the speech presented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is of great interest to all members of this House, particularly on a subject which is so near and dear to him. I think members would do well to take heed of the remarks of the member from Winnipeg North Centre on a subject about which he is so knowledgeable.
1 listened also with great interest to the speeches made by my colleagues in the House of Commons, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) and the hon. member for York-Sun-bury (Mr. Howie). Both of these gentlemen made excellent representations, and I am certain their impact will be felt in the presentation of this bill and their support of it.
I must add that I was interested to hear what the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) had to say. Probably he should know more about pensions than anybody else in the nation. Unfortunately, like most of the others in the country 1 was disappointed with his remarks. I suppose if anybody in this House of Commons should not have been dealing with that particular subject, it might be said that the member for Lincoln, who has been somewhat chatted about in recent months, should not have entered into the paiticular question of pensions.
However, I am glad to say that I can support Bill C-16, which will give a $35 increase to recipients of the GIS. But I am somewhat concerned about the method in which it was presented to the country. As hon. members are aware, this bill came about as a result of a Liberal promise made during the past election campaign, and although the fine print dealt explicitly with its being made available only to those who could pass a test, which presumably is the means test, it was in the minds of most individuals, certainly most recipients of old age security, that all people who were 65 years of age and over would be receiving the $35 increase.
For that reason I think it unfortunate that it had to come in the fashion it did, because the plight of senior citizens in Canada surely must be of more concern to the consciences of government than an election campaign. It was in that same vein that I was disappointed in the approach of the other opposition party in this House, that it too utilized senior citizens somewhat as a tool in its effort to have members elected. That is on the record, if anyone should choose to inspect it.
There were pressures on the government of the day to include that type of promise. However, we determined that we should not use senior citizens to that extent, and our decision was that the entire plight of senior citizens should be examined thoroughly and the decision would be based on a realistic evaluation of the difficulties that these people face.
By the year 2001 the number of senior citizens in Canada will have increased to about 3.4 million souls. Presently there are about 2.1 million senior citizens here. They represent approximately 12 per cent of the population. By the year 2030, we will have over 7 million senior citizens in Canada. Senior citizens are defined as those people over the age of 65. There
Old Age Security Act
will be about two to three times as many senior citizens in Canada by the year 2030 as there are now. By the year 2031, it is estimated that in Canada there will be only two people working to support one senior citizen. At the present time there are seven working people who support one pensioner.
The question that we must deal with as members of the House of Commons is to determine how these people are living and to examine their plight. I think that most of us recognize and appreciate that senior citizens are living poorly. Old age security, the guaranteed income supplement and the Canada Pension Plan account for more than one-half of the total income of people over the age of 65. Private sources-that is, private pensions-amount to something less than 12 per cent of the total income of senior citizens. In 1978, 54 per cent of recipients of the OAS were eligible for the guaranteed income supplement. That indicates that over 54 per cent of our senior citizens in 1978 were below the poverty line and were less well off than they were prior to 1978, prior to becoming senior citizens.
The average income of the elderly is about one-third that of the non-elderly. After tax considerations are taken into account, it increases to about 40 per cent. Even after the allowance for wealth, which includes such things as houses and other properties and the number in the family that they are responsible for, the gap gets narrower, but there is no question that the gap is still considerable.
Financing to support senior citizens is becoming an increasing burden on society. Today the expenditure of keeping senior citizens amounts to about 3 per cent of the total value of goods and services. By the year 2031 it is expected that the total expenditure will amount to about 7-plus per cent of the value of goods and services. It costs about three times as much in Canada to keep an elderly person as it does to maintain a child. That shoots down the argument that when the year 2031 rolls around there will be fewer children so there will be more money available to support senior citizens.
We recognize that as compassionate Canadians the objective of government has got to be the alleviation of poverty among our elderly citizens. In those terms Canada does not do such a bad job as far as other nations of the world are concerned. The only nations in the free world that exceed Canada's contribution to its elderly are Sweden, Italy and France, but in real terms, the terms that we must deal with, are they being treated fairly? The fact is that senior citizens in this country, the elderly who are recipients of old age security and guaranteed income supplement, are substantially below the minimum income standards that most of us know.
It is also interesting to note that elderly couples are better off than singles in this country. Because women live longer than men, they are worse off when living alone in unsubsidized housing. They are at the bottom of the heap, so to speak. Twenty per cent of the elderly couples in this country and 60 per cent of individuals who are senior citizens are living below the poverty line. Their plight increases every day because of

May 27, 1980
Old Age Security Act
inflation. The fact is that their pensions are based on the consumer price index. However, the CPI does not reflect that increase in the commodity which so much affects them as individuals. That of course, is primarily the price of food. It is way out of line in comparison to the CPI. For that reason, it is unfair that these pensions are indexed on the CPI scale.
We then come to the question: Can we continue to afford to support them? Can we look into the future and can we see ourselves as a nation being able to pay the bills? In this country, as I mentioned, the pension schemes include the old age security, guaranteed income supplement and Canada Pension Plan. The old age security and guaranteed income supplement are programs that are financed by taxes that are collected during the year, and the Canada Pension Plan is partially funded.
As I stated, we must not forget that it is our responsibility as legislators, as members of Parliament, as the voice for senior citizens in this House of Commons, to ensure that their poverty is not only alleviated and helped, but indeed that they are brought to a level whereby then can live as properly as they should. That is our responsibility, and I want to reinforce my support for any type of legislation that will bring these senior citizens, who in so many cases are below the poverty line, above the poverty line.
In that regard, I will support Bill C-16 although the help of $35, or $17.50 each in the case of couples, is not very much. It is a mere pittance, but it is a step in the right direction. However, this House should not regard that as being a permanent solution. Surely the government will take it upon itself to do something about the difficulties of these people before another general election is held. These are hard decisions, the financing of the plan, which must be taken now. We cannot wait until the time is upon us when we no longer have the funds to assist our senior citizens.
Some people say that all funding should come out of general revenue, that the younger generation, the people who are now in the work force, should be paying to support the older generation. With respect to the old age security and guaranteed income supplement, I can support that kind of thesis. This is the type of system we have had in this country for a good number of years. I believe there is room in our system to support this type of approach.
However, I reject it with respect to the Canada Pension Plan. It is in that regard that I believe we must take responsibility now to ensure that the Canada Pension Plan remains at a level that will alleviate the drain on the treasury which it is bound to make and will as a result affect the guaranteed income supplement when the time rolls around that there are no longer any funds left in the Canada Pension Plan.
At the present rate, by 1985 pay-outs will apparently exceed contributions. By the turn of the century, the year 2000, the fund will be depleted entirely. It is obvious to me, and I trust obvious to the government and to other members of the House, that the time is now here to adjust the formula. We must prepare for the future of our senior citizens now.
There has been some suggestion that lower retirement should be brought into play, that it should be made available to those individuals who want to opt out of the work force. The entitlement to old age security and the guaranteed income supplement has been age 65 for close to a decade. I reject the suggestion put forward by some members that the retirement age should be reduced to 60. The fact is that people are living longer in this day and age and are expected to continue to live longer as the years go by. They are living longer because they are healthier. I do not reject out of hand all cases. I think there are special instances.
I was pleased to see the previous Conservative government take steps to protect widows between the ages of 60 and 65 who lost their spouses who were over 65 and were no longer entitled to spouse's allowances. I was pleased to see that government take steps to ensure that spouses continue to receive the spouse's allowance. That is a healthy attitude. That is an attitude I feel we should see continue in this House.
I would like to plead the case for those widows who had husbands or widowers who had wives in the work force who predeceased them and who are below 60 years of age, for example age 56, 57, 58 or 59. These people have a difficult time trying to cope with life. At that age it is difficult for someone who has never had any experience in the work force to try and go out and make a living and a contribution not only to themselves, but perhaps a family as well. I would like to think this government would have compassion enough for those people that they would take into consideration the situation in which this very special group of people find themselves.
I would also like to plead the case on behalf of the families of veterans whose breadwinner, or the veteran himself, has died. Those people should be allowed a special place, an entitlement to pension benefits and to consideration from us as legislators. I feel the mandatory retirement age of 65 is no longer realistic. I would like to see that phased out. In too many instances at age 65 we have people who are prepared and able to cope with many more years of service in the work force. People need that income as a means to support their families and themselves at the level to which they are accustomed. When we force them into retirement at age 65, in too many instances we are forcing them into a state of poverty.
These people should be able to maintain their eligibility to work and their eligibility to their pensions as well. At age 65 they should continue to receive their old age security benefits. They should be allowed to continue to work if that is their decision. In a good many instances, they are competent, capable individuals. We have seen many examples in the House of Commons of individuals who have much to contribute and who have contributed much past the age of 65. Of course, the fact of the matter is that as they become more of a force, they become a more significant group in the country and, with fewer people entering the work force we are going to need their contribution.
May 27, 1980

The special Senate committee on retirement has recommended the abolition of mandatory retirement one year at a time over the next five years. 1 believe that report was published last November. 1 support that approach. 1 believe it is a realistic attitude for the nation to adopt. I would like to see this country head in that direction.
In closing, may I say that the economy needs our senior citizens. It will rely on the competence and capability of these people more and more as the years progress and I believe we should not be forcing them out. I believe we should be providing greater amounts of money to our pension scheme, the one which is partially funded at this time, the Canada Pension Plan, to ensure that there are dollars there in the years to come to continue paying out the full benefits of the plan without relying on the taxpayers of the day to do that job, and that there will be ample funds in the old age security fund and the guaranteed income supplement fund to ensure that those who do require assistance have access to funds.
The overriding consideration must surely be to bring the elderly above poverty limits. I do not believe we should use the lowest poverty limits in this country as the example; I believe we should strike a happy medium. As I have mentioned, the CPI is not a realistic index with regard to those commodities which so closely affect our senior citizens. 1 believe that these people should no longer under any circumstances have to suffer, and I primarily believe that the elderly, the senior citizens in this country, should no longer have to fear for their future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I sincerely appreciate the opportunity to speak on Bill C-16, to amend the Old Age Security Act, because it directly affects many of the people who live in my constituency. Okanagan North is a constituency which boasts very beautiful scenery and very beautiful weather. This attracts very many senior citizens. In fact, in the community in which I live, the community of Vernon, some 40 per cent of the population are senior citizens.
When passed, Bill C-16 will fulfil the government's election promise to increase the monthly guaranteed income supplement for pensioners and those receiving spouse's allowance by $35 per person. In the case of married couples, however, their pensions will increase by only $17.50 each. This was not the understanding of many among the electorate during the course of the most recent federal campaign. People are dismayed, upset and astonished, particularly married senior citizens. Surely, only the Liberal party believes the myth of the 1930s that two can live as cheaply as one.
I would like to speak for a few moments, though, on behalf of those elderly Canadians who will not receive this increase and those Canadians who need more, much more, than this increase will provide. I should like to call attention to the inequities inherent in this legislation and, indeed, in all legislation dealing with pensions in this country.
Mr. Speaker, 36.4 per cent of all Canadians age 65 and over have an annual income of less than $5,000. In 1975, 60 per cent of households in Canada headed by pensioners aged 65 and older had incomes of less than $4,000. The elderly people of this country are poor. Many of them are shockingly poor. The increase which is now proposed reflects the government's band-aid approach to vital reform, an approach which cannot continue. Increases of $35 here or $40 there over the next 20 years will not solve Canada's pension problems. We cannot expect senior citizens to be content if federal legislators continue to treat their concerns on an ad hoc basis. It is our responsibility as elected representatives to review conscientiously the situation as it exists today, recognize the inequities and, more important, act to correct the problems.
The very nature of pension financing requires that decisions be made earlier. If we are to have an effective pension program in the year 2000 we must make decisions now,

May 27, 1980
Old Age Security Act
decades before our reforms will directly affect the individual pensioner.
The changing structure of Canada's population is well documented. We are witnessing lower birth rates and lower immigration levels. If this pattern continues, and there is no reason to believe it will not, the older generation will eventually be larger than the younger. We must take this into consideration when dealing with the complicated issue of pension financing. Under current conditions, the ratio of old to young in this country will more than double between the years 1975 and 2050. If we continue the present pattern, as I suggest we shall, it can only mean it is going to cost the individual worker more and more money to support the retired population. We must now question the advisability of this situation.
I should like to take a few moments in which to outline what I believe to be one of the most urgent problems facing us today, one which the government must be prepared to deal with, and deal with now. Even a cursory examination of our public pension schemes demonstrates that we are fast approaching a crisis. The government cannot be allowed to ignore the issue of financing. History will record its attitude toward social responsibility in this area. It is a fact that the contributions scheduled under the Canada and Quebec pension plans will not be sufficient to finance pensions to which current workers are entitled. Without an increase in contributions, according to the department of insurance, the fund will be exhausted in 2003. The total contribution rate of employees and employers now equals 3.6 per cent of earnings. This must rise to 9.1 per cent by the year 2030. It is almost unnecessary to say that if future workers are unwilling or unable to pay the necessary increases in taxes and contributions, today's workers will lose all of their benefits.
By way of example of what can be done, the provincial government of British Columbia has recently moved to determine future increases in pension payments by the amount of money paid into the plan, by the amount of money contributed. The provincial government has acted to limit cost of living increases in civil servants' pensions on the understanding that open-ended indexing that is tied to the consumer price index will only result in an increased deficit. The province was worried, and justifiably so, about the unfunded liability which has been created by its own and the federal government's pension plans. These liabilities amount to $1 billion provincially and $7 billion federally.
I should point out that I am not necessarily lending my full support to the B.C. government proposal in this area. I am only saying that at least it is statistically correct, and that at least it is a fiscally responsible decision. I am not saying yes or no to the social aspect of that proposal.
This government has made a political decision to use scarce government funds-or, rather, tax moneys of Canadians-to subsidize the Canadian automobile driver. This government currently subsidizes the gas and oil consumer to the tune of some $3 billion per year. That amounts to about two hundred
tax dollars per year for every man, woman and child in this country. I realize that this government has limited funds at its disposal, although this is hardly noticeable when one considers the gay abandon with which the liberal administration spends taxpayers' dollars. As I said earlier, I realize that choices have to be made, but I am not one who would have used scarce dollars and scarce tax revenue to subsidize the driver of the automobile. Gas guzzlers are used for pleasure as well as business. If I had had to make a decision in that area, I think I would have decided to spend taxpayers' dollars on some more worthy social purpose than to provide cheap automobile transportation and encourage the over-consumption of an already scarce resource.
By way of example, I suggest that the almost $3 billion subsidy spent every year would provide a pension increase of over $1,500 a year for each pensioner in Canada. By way of another example, $3 billion would go a long way toward properly funding our present pension plans. I might add that if the $3 billion was spent in Canada rather than handed over to the oil-rich countries as it is now, that would provide an enormous boost to our economy, with resulting beneficial effects on business, productivity and employment.
I urge this government to reconsider its choices and priorities and place the needs of pensioners at a much higher level on the list.
In the throne speech this government listed its second principle of action as follows: "My ministers will help first those who need help most". It seems to me that this government has chosen to subsidize the car driver and to allow the elderly to continue to live in poverty.
What of the elderly woman in our society? Two out of three elderly women in this country have income levels which are below the poverty line; 66 per cent of all widows over 65 live at sub-poverty levels. It seems that the position of women in the pension system has been largely ignored, for perhaps a number of reasons. Perhaps it is partly because the issue of women and pensions is tied to the relationship between women and the working world. In this regard the government should act toward strengthening survivor benefits, since many private plans have little or no death benefits, and most widows' pensions amount to 50 per cent or less of pensioners' benefits. This government has to recognize the fact that $35 a month is only a small step toward providing any real relief for individuals who are forced to live at sub-poverty levels.
I would like now to express my concern to this government regarding an issue which was brought to my attention by several constituents and many other people in and around this country. I understand that this is not a peculiar problem to British Columbia but is evident across Canada. I am told that the current formula for receiving old age security and guaranteed income supplement forces those over the age of 65 who wish to get married to live together without, as we used to say, the benefit of clergy. This is most distressing to a large number of elderly people.
At the present time a married couple receives funds totalling 100 per cent of the poverty line, whereas a single pensioner
May 27, 1980

receives moneys totalling 78 per cent of the poverty line. This means that it is not, then, economically sound for two single pensioners to get married and give up up to 56 per cent of their combined income, particularly when they are living below the poverty level. This is a very real concern to many Canadians, and I speak on their behalf and on behalf of these senior citizens to encourage the government to re-evaluate this situation.
In conclusion, 1 reiterate that I support this bill and encourage its speedy passage. I am concerned, however, that the present government recognize the fact that this increase is only the first step.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to add my voice to those members who have congratulated the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) on her reappointment to her portfolio. Most certainly it is one of the most important portfolios, especially as many of its activities touch millions of our citizens in a very direct way. As time goes on, and considering some of the constitutional proposals currently in vogue, it may very well be that it will be even more important that we maintain whatever meaningful, direct contact we can between the federal government and citizens across Canada.
It is precisely because the old age security program is one of the few federal programs that touch many, many Canadians directly, along with a few other programs such as the unemployment insurance program and family allowance program, that I wish to spend most of my few minutes discussing the issue and principle of universality. Yesterday two of my colleagues, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Beaches (Mr. Young), dealt at some length with many of the other issues involved with and related to this bill, such as the continuing discrimina-

May 27, 1980
Old Age Security Act
tion against women in our current old age security system and the steps required in an attempt to end that discrimination. Second, they touched upon the fact that our pension levels are still inadequate in relation to realistic estimates of the poverty line, the history and development of pensions in Canada and the reduction of the retirement age. Also they put forward detailed proposals enunciated by our party in the recent election campaign, including our suggestion that the basic old age security pension should be increased immediately by an amount of $40 per month.
Of course, it goes without saying that 1 am in full agreement with their remarks and the proposals which they outlined, especially, their reference, and also the remarks of the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) when he spoke yesterday, urging a return to omit the principle of universality and a move away from the needs or means test.
I am very much afraid that if we allow the principle of universality to be eroded further in programs such as the old age security system, family allowances and UIC benefits, then we will sooner or later precipitate a backlash from those middle income wage earners who work hard and pay most of the tax bill in this country only to find themselves, especially in the last few years in one program after another, cut off from the very benefits for which they have been paying.
Sometimes people have a very difficult time even reaching retirement age, not to mention-depending on the type of industry they have worked in-whether they are able to enjoy that retirement for other than perhaps a very few months. I am thinking particularly of the mining industry and the logging industry with some of their environment hazards. If we continue to adopt a system that cuts off those people who pay the majority of the bill from the benefits of one program after another, then sooner or later a backlash will take place in spite of the leadership which they or their organizations have given.
The cut-off levels for some of these programs are being set almost exactly, as we watch them year by year, in tune with or just a little above the average industrial wage. In the union which I was proud to represent prior to being elected to the House of Commons, a number of us noticed for many years that every time we negotiated our wage agreement, we were within a very few dollars of where the cut-off levels were being set to deny unemployment insurance benefits, to phase out family allowances, or in some provinces to eliminate them. Because of the erosion of the basic old age security pension, that which is paid out without a needs or a means test, we do not see many of them gaining any increasing benefit from the increasing share of the tax load which they have been paying.
No matter how idealistic some of us may want to be on occasion, sooner or later these people will be driven into a more socially conservative approach in spite of their usual willingness not only to support but to lead the fight for these kinds of programs and many other social programs which very often have tended to benefit others more than themselves. I am referring to people who in some cases have not had the benefit of being able to negotiate pension programs of their own and many other benefits.
One almost begins to wonder, noticing this tendency in the last few years, whether the continuing move away from the principle of universality is consciously or unconsciously designed to set a social backlash in motion. I cannot believe that that would be the intent of the minister today. Certainly the remarks of the hon. member for Lincoln, if he reflects any body of opinion at all across the floor, would at least lead me to hope that that is not the conscious or unconscious intent. But many of us have begun to wonder. I suggest that it could not be better calculated to provoke that kind of social backlash than if it were intended.
That to me would be regrettable. It flies in the face of everything that I and my colleagues have stood for over the years. It flies in the face of the kinds of social leadership which I believe not only my colleagues but many people in other parties have advocated over a long, long period of time. It would be a move backwards in spite of some very enlightened social leadership under rather pressing conditions which Canada has been very lucky to find in the labour movement in this country over past decades. Very often they have sacrificed many of their own abilities to gain benefits for themselves in order to set into place mechanisms which would aid those citizens who have had less power to further their own ends and interests.
I do not want to say very much more, but there is a rather common phrase in my father's country of origin, Denmark, which I think is apt to many social security programs. Their hope was to build a society where "few have too much and none have too little." Unless we can move toward the principle of universality, I believe we will fly in the face of that kind of social objective. I think that would be wrong. I think it would be dangerous for the entire fabric of our society. Of course I have to support the motion before us. It will be of some help to many people. But unfortunately, perhaps it leads us even further away from the principle of universality which I and many others believe is so important to the entire social fabric and future of our country.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to say how pleased I am with the general support of this bill from speakers of all parties. Of course, I am quite pleased, as well, that members in every corner of this House have expressed the desire to do more to alleviate the financial problems of senior citizens in Canada.
The $35 a month will be a substantial increase and, according to the pleasure of the House, will start with the cheque in July. This is a total injection of about $500 million to this group of Canadians. We all know it is not enough.
May 27, 1980

Could the House please let me say, before we start discussing the details of the bill in Committee of the Whole, that I am the first one to recognize what I identify as the next step for us to take in Canada, namely, to liberate and free another sum of money. I wish the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) were here. We will liberate another sum of money as soon as the economy is in better shape and is more alive, amounting to about $730 million. That is what is missing to bring all senior citizens above the poverty line. 1 use that expression "poverty line", a cold, statistical phrase, as a measure which we can all understand and use to show our progress year after year, decade after decade, in providing a better quality of life for Canadians.
Perhaps I could answer just a few points that were made during the debate after my opening speech, and I will be very brief. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) stated that he did not agree with the approach of a conference on pensions which 1 announced or reiterated at the end of my speech. He said that when he was the minister he had plans for a comprehensive review and the reference of the whole subject area to a standing committee of this House. In this regard I would like to say that 1 am sure we both share the same objective, which is to improve pensions in Canada, particularly private pension plans. However, I am in total disagreement as to the way by which this can be achieved.
As I said, all major studies have been done on private, public, semi-public or parapublic pensions, like the CPP, except one which is being finished and is due at the beginning of next fall, and I refer to the Ontario royal commission on pensions.
What is needed? Do we need one more committee and, by the way, could a committee of the House study and put together 15 or so reports, and how would it do so? Our assessment in light of all that we know of House of Commons proceedings, with the tools of work at our disposal, with the workload of members of all parties, is that a committee of the House of Commons may not be the best tool for doing this. We think that a committee, if given such a reference, would have to take at least two, if not three, years to do the work.
What is the work to be done? It seems to me the work to be done involves a technical step; namely, putting together these studies and listing in a comparative form the various recommendations. That is what I call a technical piece of work that the committees of the House are not equipped to do. In any event, that is what our departments are for. They have the expertise and the researchers to digest these various reports and present recommendations in a summarized way. [Translation]
How should I put it? I will finish in French: having themselves put some order into all the recommendations and compared them one with another. Thus I have asked the department to prepare that table to summarize the recommendations contained in the more than twelve or fifteen reports already drafted on pensions.
Old Age Security Act
Now what is the second step we consider the most important? Action is the answer. We think it is high time that the parties concerned, the economic partners, meaning employers, governments as employers, unions and pensioners themselves publicly discuss those recommendations. We think we are ready to have Canadians, and particularly the economic partners directly involved, to start talking about the different ways they favour and those they dislike, and telling us why, and second, for the negotiation and decision-taking process to be well under way within the next two or, at the most, three years. Indeed, we thought that a committee would have lost precious time with a tool which is far from being the most appropriate for making studies and recommendations based on various reports. In conclusion, I wish to emphasize the importance of making the first steps. We believe that a national conference in the fall would be the best way to do so.

The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) made national news with something I would not like to use to make national news. It is true that it is his choice, but I would like to know why he did so. He said he believes honestly that by giving to people living alone, single, divorced, widows and widowers, a sum of money twice as great as what each partner of a couple will get will create the incentive to divorce. That seems to me to be pure fantasy, to say the least. 1 could also say that it seems to be pure Tory policy, or pure Tory belief about human nature. There is no need to say that. You do not divorce for $17 more a month. I cannot accept that. I asked the department how many divorces we created in Canada the last time we gave an increase to single people. They are very polite and they did not burst out laughing in my face, but they did not know what to tell me. To our knowledge this never happened.
I am saying, in other words, that no government has provided a sum of money which would change the behaviour of people to the point that they would choose divorce at age 65 just to get $17 more a month. I will not speak more of that, but I find that concern bizarre. I do not understand it and I do not think it is accurate. This does not happen and that is why I seem to be considering it very lightly.
Let me conclude by saying a few words about the statements of my friends in the New Democratic Party. I listened very carefully and have reviewed rapidly, though not in depth yet, all the possible indicators of inflation which can be used in indexing pensions. The results would indicate there would only be a few pennies, at most $1 or $2 more or less every three months. I will continue to explore the question to make sure there are not significant benefits lost to the seniors because of our way of indexing their pensions. The question I will pose to

May 27, 1980
Old Age Security Act
my department 1 am already aware of, because it is the question that will give me the answer. The question is: If we were to choose a different way of indexing instead of the way we do it in Canada now, how many more millions of dollars will it cost initially? When I get the answer I will know immediately if we are talking business, if we are talking of something very serious, or if we are talking of a nuance with so little relevance it could not really affect the lives of our seniors.
During this debate I listened carefully to the members of the New Democratic Party who spoke and particularly, of course, to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I remember very clearly the promises of that party during the last election campaign. Only today did I come to the conclusion that they speak the way they do because it is a strategy to maintain universality. I came to that understanding only today, and I am not even sure of my observations.
Quite honestly, I had great difficulty understanding the sudden promise of the NDP party during the election campaign, that they wanted to raise the basic OAS pension for every Canadian by $40 a month. Such an increase would amount to $2.5 billion a year. That is a huge figure. I was very surprised at this promise because there was no consensus in Canadian society that such an urgent step was required. There is this urgency in certain quarters, among specialists and experts, but not among the general public.
The idea that the general basic OAS pension should be slightly higher in order to correspond to, for example, 15 per cent of industrial wages or to some other measure is a theoretical concept developed among specialists. To my knowledge, this opinion has never reached the Canadian public and surely there is no consensus of urgency. For me the consensus of urgency is giving those pensioners on the GIS-in other words, those who need it-a better deal. The measure being used to make sure that there is a unique message, one which we keep repeating in order to achieve success, is: "Bring them above the poverty line". That is what we are trying to do with this bill.
As I said, one more step is required before these people will be brought completely above the poverty line. This time we are coming closer to that realization with the sum of $.5 billion. Another large sum of money will be required to make sure that they are brought over that poverty line once and for all. So if it was not an election campaign promise, I would say to the NDP members what I have already told them in public, that they have the academics but they still need an accountant in their party. One cannot find $2.5 billion just like that.
If I stress this point, it is because the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen) spoke often of the need for returning to the principle of universality. The hon. member does not know it, but he has raised the scarecrow of the loss of universality in old age pensions and, by way of consequence, family allowances. I think that this is the strategy of that party. That party wants to raise the OAS pension issue to put
back into the minds of the Canadian public the need for saving pensions for all.
I can tell the hon. member that that is a battle which was won just a few months ago. I honestly think that members of this House from the government, the New Democratic Party and others who were interested in the fight in favour of maintaining universality against the trend of neo-conservatism which Canada, as well as other countries in the western world, has already gone through was won last fall and during Christmas and that it is now a battle of the past. I am very pleased about that.
I have no reason to believe that universality of social programs is under question, under fire or in threat of being lost. I must insist on that point because it takes so much energy to win such a battle, and I prefer to save my energy for the next battle. The hon. member for Kootenay West was talking about a battle of the past, and that does not interest me much. I prefer to identify the next step and tell Canadians that the next time we will have to do more for those people who have reached the age of 65 and who are living in conditions of poverty.
I do not want to leave Canadians today with the slightest hope that the basic old age pension will increase. Well into the future, the next step will probably be to help those people who are between the ages of 62 and 65. That will be the next step, to help those in need within that age group.
At this point I would like to thank all those who participated in the debate. Many hon. members were kind enough to agree to a speedy passage of this bill and to reserve their remarks for other occasions. I ask all hon. members of this House, whatever their political party or political beliefs, because they have all said nice things about the need to combat poverty among senior citizens, that they give their help by any means at their disposal and, particularly, help obtain from the provinces a commitment that this $35 will be passed on to all senior citizens living in institutions.

I think it is important for recipients of the pension to know that their increase will be in the cheque they receive at the end of July and not in the cheque they receive toward the end of June which they spend in the month of July.
I think it is also important and useful that it has been made clear that anyone who is getting any portion of the supplement at the present time, even if it is only $1 per month, will get the $35 in the case of a single person or $17.50 each in the case of two members of a married relationship.
Before I get into the one or two questions that 1 should like to put to the minister, I should like to say a word or two. I am not going to indulge in a long speech about our relative philosophies in this area but I was pleased that the minister, when she made her speech and tried to get straight in her own mind what our strategy is, said categorically that the battle for universality has been won-that no one is going to go back on that.
I hope the hon. member for Bow River heard that. When he made his speech yesterday, he said that he used to believe in universality but that he does not any more. He wants to take it away from some of those at the top of the scale, supposedly to enrich the pension to others. I trust the battle is won but there are still a few stragglers around who think they would like to change that principle. I agree with the minister as to its importance, and my colleagues and I feel very strongly about universality.
I was glad to hear the statements made last night by the hon. member for Lincoln, and I suspect that there are other Liberals on that side who have the same view. Likewise, I remind the minister again of my approval yesterday of the statements in this connection made by Senator David Croll on the occasion when a testimonial dinner was held for him over in the West Block.
It is still my view, Mr. Chairman, that it is wrong to make persons prove their poverty to get additional money. I think it is better for the amount to be paid universally and for the income tax to be used much more steeply than it is now to take it back from those at the top. However, that is an ongoing issue and we can discuss it time and time again, on and off the
record. As I say, I am satisfied to let that part of the discussion end for today with the minister's ringing declaration that universality is here to stay. Let it be that way for sure.
Taking the bill as it is, namely a bill that does not increase the basic rate of the old age security pension but increases only the amount of the guaranteed income supplement, there are two or three questions I should like to put to the minister.
In the first place, I should like to ask her whether she and her department are giving study to some other basis for establishing the guaranteed income supplement level than that which we now have. I am inclined to agree with her that we put too much blame on the method of indexing. We say that it is wrong and that it does not produce the right results, but is not the real trouble that the base was too low at the start? It is no use for government members to say we have got indexing so we keep the pension value up where it was, when to begin with it was too far down.
What about my suggestion the other day that, instead of starting with a figure just drawn out of a hat and then indexing it, we start with a figure that bears some relationship to the cost of living at the level sometimes defined as the poverty line?
As I say, for the veterans on the disability pension, we have established a formula. We get away from it at times, but it is there and we keep coming back to it, namely that the 100 per cent disability pension shall be the average take-home pay of five designated categories in the public service. Why not establish, I said the other day, 125 per cent of the poverty level as the line below which no pensioner should be allowed to fall, and then either index that to the consumer price index or index it to the changes in the poverty level as established by Statistics Canada?
As the minister knows, when we take that computation we are taking the lowest one around. Any social agency will produce a level that is higher and, of course, there are problems about different costs in city and in country. But surely something better than just a figure drawn out of a hat, that no indexing ever makes adequate, would be better. I would like to ask the minister, when I give her a chance to reply, if she will tell me whether some study is being given to that in her department.
Second, I ask the minister, and I press this upon her as strongly as I can, whether in this term of office she is enjoying she is going to do something about the disgrace of the spouse's allowance legislation. The original motive may have been good-to give something to people who needed it. But the result is for women between 60 and 65 for the most part-I know it works both ways but there are not very many men involved-there is applied a marital test. If a woman has a man or has one that dies while she is in that age bracket, she gets the pension. But if she does not have a man because she is a spinster or divorced or became a widow before age 60, or she became a widow before her husband was over 65, there is no pension there.
May 27, 1980

The other day when I was talking about this, one of the Tory members here tried to chide me a bit. He thought I was actually standing up and advocating a means or an income test. I am not, and the minister knows that. But surely in that 60 to 65 age bracket something in the nature of a supplement or a pension because people need it is far more civilized, far more modern, than this pension based on the test that is applied to every woman, namely, has she got a man? It just does not wash any more. There is not a doubt in my mind that the minister does not like it. She was not connected with this department when this test was brought in; she was in a more esoteric area, the area of external affairs. I often wonder what she thought about the test when it was being put through. My urgent plea to her is that something be done about this.
We heard comments made today when the minister was turning down our request for an increase in the basic amount of the pension, at least turning us down for now. There is always the future in this business and there are the increases that come about because of the rise in the cost of living. Anyway, when she was doing that she said that the area where something was needed to be done was that respecting unattached women-I think the age bracket she gave was 62 to 65.
I would rather see the bracket of 60 to 65, and there is the problem of those from 55 up. That is where the problem assumes rather large proportions.
I was glad to hear the minister say that, just as I was glad to hear her say that the battle for universality has been won. But I relate this to the unfairness in the spouse's allowance. What is she going to do to meet this problem which all of us know is so real? We can give our statistics about pensioners, we can tell about the problems that people have, single or married, in large cities, and all the rest of it, and I can make my speeches about the desirability of universality. But I agree with her that the most pressing problem for senior citizens is the problem faced by unattached women from 60 to 65, as well as those between 55 and 60. I hope that the minister will tell us that the department is going to do something more about that area than is done in this bill.
I had another question down. I was going to leave it to my friend from Victoria, but he mentioned it in his second reading speech although he did not raise it again in Committee of the Whole. But with my respect for him, since he comes from a place where so many of them are involved-I know from the correspondence I get from the member's constituency-I will raise the matter, and that is this question of reciprocity.
