subsubtopic: AMENDMENT PROHIBITING PUBLICATION OF IDENTITY OF ACCUSED PERSONS
speechtext:
that Bill C-213, to amend the Criminal Code (reporting names of accused), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise today to address myself to this topic and to this bill in particular. I naturally hope that this bill might go to the committee for consideration and will not be talked out. I happen to think that the subject matter at least is very important; it is one that we have shied away from addressing straight on. 1 hope there will be some exposure of it today. Maybe it could be dealt with at length in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
I first introduced this bill back on July 12, 1977. I introduced it again on October 29, 1979. Interestingly enough, I find that in the provincial legislature of Ontario, Albert Roy, the provincial member for Ottawa East, copied the principle of this bill and introduced one of his own back in November, 1977, and had it debated in that assembly. It is more appropriate to debate this bill in this House and to amend the Criminal Code.
First, I would like to refer to section 2, subsection (f) of the Bill of Rights, which states that a person charged with a criminal offence has the right, and I quote:
-to be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law in a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal-
I agree with that 100 per cent. I might also point out in advance of going into the details of my comments today that 1 have received opinions in support of this bill from such diverse groups as the South Okanagan civil liberties society and the report of the committee of the social planning council of Ottawa-Carleton concerning the publication of the names of persons accused of crimes.
A lot of the detail I will go into comes from a magistrate in England, Magistrate Margaret Jones, who in 1974 did quite a lengthy paper, which was her thesis for her Ph.D., dealing with this topic of whether or not there should be broadcasting or printing in the printed news media of people's names prior to their having been convicted.
I am pleased that today we will have an opportunity of considering this bill. The bill is designed to recognize one of
the fundamental concepts on which our system of justice is based, and that is that an accused is presumed innocent until proved guilty. Toward that end, this bill would prevent the naming of an accused in the media until he or she is convicted of an offence. Since 1 first introduced this bill I have received many letters, some from journalists, some from civil liberties groups, and some from individuals who felt that they suffered unjustly because they had their names appear in the local media only to be subsequently acquitted of the charge.
I believe this bill is quite straightforward. It would prevent the publication or broadcasting of the name, address or occupation of an accused in any manner in connection with the commission of an offence or the judicial proceedings arising out of the commission of such an offence. For the purposes of the bill, I have defined an accused as anyone who has been charged with an offence and who is awaiting trial, undergoing trial, has been acquitted, or has received an absolute discharge or pardon.
I realize that this bill is not perfect, that the argument surrounding the question of a free press versus a free trial is not about to be resolved this afternoon. The files I have compiled and the letters I have received on this bill have shown just how divided public opinion is on this issue, even among sectors such as the civil liberties groups which usually have no problem finding a consensus.
Basically I have introduced this bill almost as a devil's advocate. I am willing to be persuaded now as to whether we should continue with the system which we presently have where people's names can appear in the press prior to conviction, or whether this bill should be passed, or at least go to committee for detailed consideration of whether persons' names should be commented upon before there is a conviction.
I hope the bill will not be talked out because it is a non-partisan issue. I believe it is a topic which does merit further study in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I hope that at least the subject matter will later today be referred to that standing committee.
In Canada, there is no encompassing standard for court reporting. Coverage is randomly selective, based on a vague notion of newsworthiness, a notion which could never be defined unanimously by any group of ten editors that one could assemble. There are only two common qualities to cases which are deemed to be newsworthy: first, it is a selective process, and secondly, it is the product at the discretion of the news editor's judgment. Unfortunately in journalism, as in all other fields, selectivity leaves the door open first for injustice, and secondly for exploitation. Perhaps the greatest irony in this debate is that while judges have strived over the years to achieve a greater consistency in sentencing, the press has achieved anything but consistency in their coverage and in their decision of what is of importance and interest to the general public.
Magistrate Margaret Jones of Britain, who has written a doctoral thesis on the subject of naming of accused, has characterized the practice of the British press as "the arbitrary infliction of publicity on a random cross-section of the
May 27, 1980

accused". It is a characterization that easily adapts itself on this side of the Atlantic. Canadian practice is a hodge-podge of guidelines and traditions and editorial edicts from each and every news organ in this country. In some cases, it is the practice not to cover shoplifting, petty theft, wilful damage under $50 and so on, but the ban gets lifted should there be a significant "human interest angle". Most editors will agree that "little crime by little people" does not deserve coverage, that is unless there is a possibility of a person's misery becoming a human interest anecdote for the lighter side.
I would like to say that this is a moral issue, and in its defence the press uses moral arguments. 1 intend to look at these, but I would like to say that first and foremost the press is an industry. Criminal proceedings are but one more source of grist for the information mills. It is the task of the media to use every available pool of information to make a selection of stories, which are then displayed in a particular order to make as good a newspaper story or broadcast as possible.
A court case is no different from any other type of story. The decisions made about coverage remain journalistic, nonjudicial. In general, the sexiness or saleability of a story is paramount. A morals charge, in practice, receives automatic attention. Leaving the scene of an accident will not, unless it is in connection with an accident of major proportions or involves a socially or politically prominent individual. An accused may see published not only his or her name, but address, occupation and even, perhaps, parentage if such happens to be newsworthy.
In this city a few years ago a case involving an alleged male prostitution ring made every front page and newscast. Many of the alleged clients were charged and their names and addresses were published. There was a preliminary hearing. It was lengthy. Then they went to trial, but prior to that one of the accused committed suicide after receiving death threats and harassment at work. So here in this city at least one death has resulted from this journalistic practice. Eventually, Mr. Speaker, all the accused were acquitted, the Crown withdrawing the charges because they did not depend upon the reliability of their young witnesses. But many of the accused had already lost their jobs or been obliged to leave the city to re-establish elsewhere because of the penalty of publicity.
Recently there has been another case in this city involving a trial for rape. The accused, who was later convicted, had not only his name, address and occupation published, but his racial origin as well. Somewhere along the line his race was deemed as integral to his trial and as newsworthy. For years the Ontario human rights commission has bluntly said that the needless accentuation of racial or ethnic origin in court reporting can only lead to the polarization of communities and suspicion. It cannot help but reinforce negative stereotypes.
As Morris Schumiatcher, chairman of the civil liberties section of the Canadian Bar Association has said, the presence at any trial of the general public, of which the press is a part, is intended to ensure a fair trial. Let us not forget that it is the
Criminal Code
accused who is supposed to be the prime beneficiary. It is not for the purpose of informing, entertaining or titillating the general public. I do not accept for one moment that the actions and the proceedings of the police or of law enforcement agencies and the courts cannot be fully and effectively reported or even commented upon in the media, but this should be done without the use of names or any other identifying description.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, the press uses moral arguments in its own defence. There is a notion that the adverse publicity is a deterrent to crime, although the reporting itself is random and there is no way of knowing with certainty what will be reported. There is a notion that the press is the instrument of the public's right to know, although there is hedging as to when knowledge crosses the boundary into curiosity or entertainment. There are even some who use the argument that publicity, should, in effect, be part of the penalty for crime, although it is not determined why an accused who is later acquitted should have to pay that penalty.
Then there is the justification which is offered that every newspaper tries to follow up on its court stories, and that where there is an acquittal that, too, will be published. But of course, Mr. Speaker, there is no guarantee that the follow-up will receive the same prominence as the initial story; nor is there any admission that with today's large urban centres and the proliferation of courts, remands and appeals, it is virtually impossible even for the most well-meaning editor to ensure that there will be an efficient follow-up on every story, particularly in connection with minor cases.
There is also the argument, taken up by several civil liberties groups, that failure to name an accused puts in the hands of the police the potential to arrest an individual, charge him, hold him in jail and neglect to notify anybody that an arrest has been made. To that 1 say "balderdash," because the same procedure could be used as is used today, only you could not disseminate the names and other identifying information. You would have the same police dockets and the remands would be the same-no more than eight days.
Some see a bill such as this one as an attempt to legislate secrecy in the courts. I do not buy that. That is not the reason for this bill. Others quite bluntly say that there is no place for sentiment in selecting court or crime stories for publication, that it is the media's obligation to report any story it feels will be important or interesting, or both, to the general public. It is funny how the names of Jean Marchand or Louis Robichaud were both on the front pages of Ottawa newspapers when they were facing charges for impaired driving. Yet any day you can go down to No. 1 court at 60 Waller Street, where the remanding is done, and find 30 or 40 people picked up every night and charged with impaired driving. But their names are not to be found even on page 60 of the same newspapers.
These arguments are the ones most often used in defence of the practice of naming the accused. I would like briefly to outline what the practice is in two European countries, countries which are frequently held up to us as models of social justice and progressive thinking.

May 27, 1980
Criminal Code
In The Netherlands the names of accused are not broadcast or published at any stage during criminal proceedings-arrest, during trial, even on sentencing or acquittal. This is a matter of tradition in the Dutch press. Where a trial story is used by the media, an accused is identified by initials. The Netherlands government is obliged to list the names of accused and the disposition of each and every case in an official government periodical.
In Sweden a code of conduct has been established by the code of honour of the press which is observed by all its members. The code states that the name of a person involved in judicial proceedings cannot be published or broadcast until conviction and sentencing, and only then if the sentence is one of imprisonment for two years or more.
Here in Canada we have seen action taken already in terms of press reporting of court cases. Reporting of preliminary inquiries as covered by section 467 of the Criminal Code states:
Prior to commencement of taking of evidence at a preliminary inquiry, the justice holding the inquiry shall, if application therefor is made by the accused, or where there is more than one accused, by any one of these, make an order directing that the evidence taken at the inquiry shall not be published in any newspaper before such time as
A)	the accused who made the application discharged, or
B)	if the accused who made the application is committed for trial or ordered to stand trial, the trial is ended.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, under sections 441 and 442 of the Criminal Code, justices have a limited jurisdiction to hold certain proceedings in camera and to exclude the public where a juvenile is charged, or where the judge is of the opinion that it is in the interests of public morals, the maintenance of order or the proper administration of justice to exclude the general public.
I should also point out that in September, 1978, the Canadian Bar Association passed the following resolution at its Halifax annual meeting:
Be it resolved that the Criminal Code be amended to provide that the name or identity of a person (including a corporation) charged with an offence shall not be published in a newspaper, magazine or periodical or broadcast in any manner unless
(a)	an indictment has been preferred pursuant to section 507 of the Criminal Code;
(b)	the accused has been committed to stand trial following a preliminary inquiry;
(c)	the trial has commenced;
(d)	the accused consents in writing to the name or identity being published or broadcast.
The purpose of that resolution was to protect those who are charged but who never come to trial for lack of evidence.
In 1974, the Ontario Press Council solicited views on the naming of an accused from the Elizabeth Fry Society and the John Howard Society.
Mrs. Elizabeth Haslam, the director of the Elizabeth Fry Society in Toronto, responded, and I quote:
We are interested in the debate about the publishing of a name as a protection against arbitrary arrest and court procedures. Personally I would see the fact of courts being open to the public, including the press, as being the safeguard. If an individual wished to have his or her name published in connection with the case, then this, of course, should be his or her right.
Mrs. Haslam also said that in her understanding of the problem, the consequences of naming an accused were worst in small communities, that the family of an accused does suffer unfairly from the practice and that the general public, contrary to our concept of presumed innocence, operates on the assumption of guilt once an accused's name is published. She also noted that in the case of the young, rather than having a deterrent effect, being named in the media is far more likely to create a sense of importance or celebrity.
At the same time, the Ontario executive director of the John Howard Society replied that the society is just as concerned about the nature and extent of crime in a community as it is with the judicial process. Here again, one wonders how a community can be served, given the selective nature of court reporting, with an accurate concept of crime within a community. There is perhaps far more constructive work to be done on the part of the media in terms of analytical crime reporting or judicial reporting than in the selective display of random cases.
In contrast, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association has taken the view that media coverage and the naming of an accused is a safeguard against abuse and remains the essential public means of evaluating government and law enforcement agencies.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you and other members of the House. I will try to wind up my remarks as quickly as possible.
As I was saying, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association has taken the view that media coverage and the naming of an accused is a safeguard against abuse and remains the essential public means of evaluating government and law enforcement agencies. The view is one of "better to run the risk of having an individual's reputation injured from time to time than have the channels of mass communication cut off'.
I would like to return to the thesis of Magistrate Margaret Jones. Mrs. Jones came from a family with a journalistic background and is married to an editor. In her book "Justice and Journalism" she states:
I have ended, after several years of study, with the conclusion that the current action of the British press in reporting the proceedings of magistrate's court is socially undesirable and detracts from the administration of justice. I have found that it contributes to injustice in its arbitrary infliction of the punishment of publicity, often the cruelest and most harmful of all penalties, upon a random selection of offenders .. . whom the newspapers choose to identify.
May 27, 1980

In her analysis Mrs. Jones said that the foundation for change would be based on modifying the nature of reporting to accord with the concept that an accused is presumed innocent as well as providing for the names of the accused and court decisions to be publicly available in a government document.
She also outlined the following three steps:
(1)	In reporting summary proceedings, there should be no publication of names or identifying particulars until a criminal charge has been determined;
(2)	In the reporting of summary proceedings, there should be no publication of names or identities when a trial ends in an acquittal unless the defendant opts for the advertisement of his or her innocence;
(3)	In the reporting of summary proceedings, there should be no publication of names or identifying particulars of civil offenders whom a court has found it expedient to punish and in respect of whom it has made an order of absolute or conditional discharge or probation unless those persons opt for identification.
As I have said before, the media is an industry, and court reporting is but one of the many materials it uses. In this country it is a tradition of reporting the names of the accused. In the past we have legislated against industries where we have found their traditions to be harmful, whether through environmental regulations or child labour laws. We have legislated such practices out of existence. I think it is time that we began to look at this segment, for if there is one point of unanimous agreement among the media, it is their distaste for guidelines laid down by any press council. And it is all too apparent that the various press councils in existence are handicapped in their efforts to police their members.
In closing, I would like to leave the last words to Margaret Jones. After publishing her thesis, she was asked to speak before the British Guild of Editors. She said:
This then is the challenge for the watchdogs of justice-do not degenerate into the jackals or hyenas of justice. In your reports of judicial proceedings can you not cease to be the hounders of humanity, at least for its minor crimes, yet still continue to watch over and record the process of justice? If you could do so you would make good the proud boast of the press that, through it, justice in our courts is seen to be done. Then you might better be called not the watchdogs but the guardians of justice; for you would show yourselves to be not dogs, but men.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to commence by congratulating the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) for raising this important subject not only on this occasion but in a number of other Parliaments as well. May I say at the outset, on behalf of the New Democratic Party, that we would support the reference, at the very least, of the subject matter of this bill to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I certainly hope hon. members opposite will agree at least to support the reference of the subject matter to that committee.
I say that we would support the subject matter being referred because, quite frankly, we have a number of concerns with regard to the bill as it is presently worded. There are some segments and areas of the bill with which we must take issue. There is certainly a fundamental safeguard which we believe should be inserted in the bill, which I will be coming to in short order.
It is clear that the matter with which we are dealing today is one of central importance to all Canadians because it essen-
Criminal Code
daily touches on two fundamental freedoms which in some senses tend to clash in this particular instance. These freedoms were both won through long and hard struggles. I refer, of course, to freedom of the press, on the one hand, and the right of the accused to a fair trial, on the other.
We have to attempt essentially to pick between these two principles and, in doing so, to come to a compromise between them, because we are really talking here about a matter of compromise. If we were to forgo the one and accept totally the other, we would be permitting, I suggest, a very serious miscarriage of justice to take place.
What the bill proposed by the hon. member attempts to do is arrive at a compromise between these two important principles. Unfortunately, I do not believe he has succeeded in doing that in the wording which is before the House at the present time. As I have said, I certainly sympathize with the objective of the bill, which is to ensure that an accused person has the right to a fair and unprejudiced trial which is decided strictly on the basis of the evidence presented before the court.
Of course, as my hon. friend has stated, the fundamental principle which must govern in criminal trials is the overriding presumption of the innocence of all accused. We have seen too many cases in which there have been reports of accused persons who have subsequently been acquitted, having had their reputations tarnished and in some cases their whole livelihoods destroyed as a result of the kind of reporting which has taken place regarding the crimes which they were alleged to have committed. I need only point to the most recent instance of this in the case of Alan Spraggett, a gentleman who was charged with very serious offences in the province of Manitoba. He lost his job, his reputation was severely tarnished, and he was subsequently acquitted by a provincial court judge. He was said to have been an honourable man, as I recall the words of Magistrate Dubienski in Manitoba.
In Canada we are fortunate to have won these fundamental principles of freedom of the press and the right to be presumed innocent to which my friend referred, in the Canadian Bill of Rights. We have to guard these principles. We have to safeguard them against both the state and the police. We have to safeguard against the effects of malicious, irresponsible or sensational reporting and comment. I appreciate that is the intent of my hon. friend's bill. Certainly I welcome his concern and share his concern for this vital right of Canadian citizens.
My hon. friend alluded to some of the conflicts within the various civil liberties groups on this question. It is not an easy question. Certainly for that reason I believe it would be inappropriate to refer the bill in its present form to committee. However, I think the fact that there is such a controversy and such a widespread interest in the subject matter of this bill warrants the referral of the subject matter to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
However, I have stated that we have some concerns. I should like to just deal briefly with those concerns. I have no intention of speaking for the full time allotted to me because I

hope members opposite will see fit to have this bill moved on to committee. The concerns I have with respect to the bill are fundamentally this: first, that there is no option on the part of the accused to insist in some cases on publication of the name of the accused. If this bill is aimed at protecting the rights of the accused, then surely it should be up to the accused to waive the provisions of non-publication. For example, if the accused believes that he or she is being harassed or intimidated, that certain aspects of the judicial process are unsatisfactory, and wants his or her name to be published together with the circumstances, it is my view that that should be at the option of the accused, because it is a bill which is essentially aiming at protecting the rights of the accused. If this bill came to committee I suspect my hon. friend would not be adverse to such a provision being inserted in the bill, but he will appreciate that as it stands now there is no such protection afforded to accused persons.
The concern expressed not only by the Canadian Civil Liberties Association but by others is precisely that this would tend to blanket the proceedings of the court and make the court proceedings more secretive. I would suggest that by amendment along the lines I have proposed, permitting accused persons themselves to have the final word as to whether or not there should be publicity of their trials, would adequately deal with the concerns these various civil liberties groups have expressed. I should say I have taken the opportunity to canvass a number of people who have indicated a concern with the bill in its present form. Without exception they have stated that with the amendment I am proposing the bill would be satisfactory. We certainly feel the persons who are accused of an offence must be assured the right to full public scrutiny of the process of law. They must be able to appear publicly to show that they have not been harmed, for example, while they were being held in custody. They must be able to have the evidence and the circumstances of their case heard publicly if they so desire, to ensure that the evidence and the process conform to the due process of law.
What we have to avoid at all costs is any suggestion that there will be any increase in the arbitrary powers which already exist in the prosecutional arm of the state. For example, we have seen the abuses of section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act. Certainly we on this side welcome the intention of the government to repeal that particular section of the Federal Court Act which has been abused far too frequently by previous governments and, I might add, by the present government, unfortunately by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) only two months ago.
Those are the kinds of provisions which we believe should be removed from the present statutes of the country. On the other hand, as I have said, we recognize the concern on the part of those persons who are accused of criminal offences that too often their trial is conducted in the newspaper, or on television, or over the radio, and even if they are found to have been not guilty of the offence with which they are charged, that in the mind and in the eye of the public in fact they are guilty, with all the consequences that holds in terms of their jobs, their
reputations, and the reputations of their families, friends and associates in the community. We recognize that that is a concern with which this particular bill is attempting to deal.
I will just pass over some of the comments I was planning on making with respect to the Official Secrets Act and trials that are being held in secret, because I think it is important the subject matter of this bill be referred. As I say, we are concerned about the question of the right of the accused to waive provisions of the bill. Also I would like to express at this point a concern with the wording of the bill. It would also ban the publication under all circumstances of the names, addresses or occupations of accused persons even after their trials have taken place, if they were acquitted or if they received an absolute discharge or pardon. Again I think my hon. friend would recognize some of the difficulties in these aspects of the bill. For example, in the case of pardons, they are not granted in some cases until a number of years after the accused has been convicted of an offence. According to the wording of the bill as it stands now, if the press reported the name of the accused in the interim between the time of conviction and the time of granting of pardon, they would be guilty of an offence. I am sure that is not the intent of the bill, but once again there are problems in the drafting of the bill as it now stands.
At this point I am not persuaded that it is a wise step to take to deny the press the opportunity to publish the names, occupations, and other relevant details of an accused person after the trial has taken place. I recognize that some of the unfortunate aspects of publication which are dealt with before the acquittal still arise here, but I believe at least at this point that the interests of the freedom of the press in that particular instance outweigh the other concerns that have been expressed. Following a trial, whether that trial results in an acquittal or a conviction, the press should be free to report on the outcome of the trial in its fullest detail.
Also I believe it is important that this be done and that there be an opportunity to report in the case of absolute discharges. I note there is no reference to conditional discharges here, but it is important that this be done in the case of discharges or acquittals, because frequently it is the case that trial judges, while acquitting an accused, or giving an accused an absolute or conditional discharge, will make certain comments with respect to the conduct of the accused. They will say that they are acquitting the accused but only on the narrowest of technical grounds. There may be important statements in the judgment of that particular accused which the public should know. While they may have been acquitted, in some instances the judge will state quite clearly his or her disapproval of the conduct of the particular accused. Surely it is the right of the public to be made aware of those kinds of concerns on the part of our judiciary.
I should like to conclude by saying that I would hope, because of the importance of the subject matter which is before the House today, which has been raised in a number of instances, and has been widely discussed by a variety of important institutions and organizations in our society, that
May 27, 1980

the subject matter of this bill would be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I am confident, if it is referred to that committee, that some of the problems I have raised in connection with its drafting will be cleared up, and those problems, having been cleared up, that we on this side of the House would be prepared to support the amended bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT PROHIBITING PUBLICATION OF IDENTITY OF ACCUSED PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) for bringing this bill forward. The matter is one which might be considered nonpartisan, an act to amend the Criminal Code reporting names of accused. At the outset I would merely suggest that there are many points of view on it and that there are many different ways of looking at it. 1 hope to bring forth some of those views this afternoon.
Also I should like to say that the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) talked about the civil liberties involved and the balancing of various freedoms. This, of course, is something that is of the utmost importance. We have to consider freedom of the press as well as the freedom to which the individual is entitled. When the hon. member talks about the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) using section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act, 1 would merely say to him that as long as the law is there it can be used, although it is my understanding that there will in fact be a change, and that particular section 41(2) will probably be repealed in the not too distant future.
With regard to the bill before us today, it seems to me at the outset it is necessary to consider the validity of the premise on which the bill is based. The explanatory note in Bill C-213 states:
The purpose of this bill is to recognize more fully the time-honoured right of an accused in Canada to be presumed innocent until proved guilty by prohibiting the media from identifying an accused unless and until he is convicted.
The validity of this premise is in doubt, for a number of reasons. First, 1 would say it assumes that trial by the media is a general occurrence. You may or may not agree with this, but I think that is a fair assumption that can be made. Second, it assumes that the present laws and processes in the criminal justice system are inadequate to prevent those rare cases of excessive or improper pre-trial publicity, which is obviously not the case. Third, it ignores the need to balance the competing social and legal interests which are involved, namely, the potential harm to the individual accused's reputation or economic interests versus society's overwhelmingly great interest in ensuring that the operation of the criminal justice system is carried out with the greatest publicity and scrutiny, with some few well recognized exceptions such as juvenile proceedings, national security, and matters of that nature.
Professor Allan Mewett lists six reasons justifying the overwhelmingly greater social and legal interests in ensuring public trial, including media publication. I will just mention them to
Criminal Code
you. They are, first, an open trial provides some safeguards against unjust or unfair proceedings against an accused; second, it militates against the use by the executive of the courts to achieve its own ends; third, it reduces the possibility of any abuse of judicial power; fourth, it maximizes the chance of equal and impartial administration of justice to all accused persons; fifth, many aspects of the enforcement of criminal law, such as general abhorrence of certain acts or general deterrence, demand that the public be informed; and, sixth, witnesses who have to give their testimony in public will be more reluctant to give false evidence for fear of exposure.
Coming back to the other details, the validity of this premise is in doubt because it gives undue weight to, or alternatively confuses the effects of publication of the identity of persons charged in relation to the consequences such persons must or are likely to suffer, although their innocence is subsequently established, because it is not possible to prevent total dissemination of the knowledge of charges and the identities of persons charged; it is not possible to prevent persons who know of the charge and identity of persons charged from drawing wrong conclusions; it is not possible to prevent some damage to the reputation or economic interests of persons who are charged with criminal offences, whether or not media publicity takes place, even if they are subsequently proven innocent; and, it ignores the educative, moral and deterrent effects of openness of the criminal justice system to the public.
It would seem that the real objective of the bill is concerned with the protection of the reputation and economic interests of a few persons who, having been charged and having received some publicity in the media, are subsequently found to be innocent or, at worst, who although convicted either receive an absolute discharge or a pardon, as the case may be. The assumption that the presumption of innocence is not being honoured sufficiently is incorrect. The presumption of innocence is too well entrenched in the Canadian criminal justice system to be assailed for the reasons stated in the explanatory note of this bill and, as will be seen later, the consequences of implementing these proposals.
What about the content and effectiveness of Bill C-213 itself? There is a blanket prohibition in the terms proposed which is not unusual in the Criminal Code or other federal statutes, such as section 142(2) of the Juvenile Delinquents Act. However, one must consider whether the interests which prevailed, in the case of the Juvenile Delinquents Act, for example, over the wider social and legal interests, should now be extended to provide no publicity in all criminal cases.
A total prohibition against media publication for all criminal offences might not be regarded as objectionable as, for example, a total prohibition excluding the public from all criminal proceedings. However, a number of factors have to be considered in the context of the effectiveness of this version of prohibition, the effect of this prohibition on the wider social and legal interests presently served by media publication, and the difficulties of application or implementation.
The true meaning of public trial is inextricably linked to full media publication of all the particulars sought to be prohibited

May 27, 1980
Criminal Code
by this very bill. This is not to say that the law does not recognize specific exemptions to the principle of publicity which are founded on specific public interest issues which are deemed of a higher order than the interest of publicity. Unfortunately, Bill C-213 creates a blanket prohibition without addressing the issues and concerns enumerated above. Such a blanket prohibition would derogate from the principle that justice must not only be done but must manifestly be seen to be done.
The total prohibition will not preclude some dissemination, because word of mouth and court room spectators will still be able to connect the accused and the charge; the facts of the charge or proceedings will continue to be the subject of publication; and the publication of the facts without particulars enabling identification may increase interest and greater speculation and rumour-mongering.
The consequences of these developments may continue to introduce a degree, albeit less than media publication, of the harms which Bill C-213 is intended to remedy, namely, protection of reputation and prevention of prejudice. In fact Bill C-213 may result in new prejudices; for example, completely innocent people may be mistakenly regarded as being involved or even as the unnamed accused as a result of speculation unchecked by fair and accurate media publication. This tendency may progress to such an extent that it brings the system of justice into disrepute.
The beneficial effects of openness, made manifest by media publication, accrue to the public, the accused and the prosecution, and would be greatly diminished by virtue of the prohibition in Bill C-213. The accused and the Crown are assisted by openness to the extent that witnesses are constrained to be more truthful, are induced to come forward, and reputations may also be vindicated. Concealing the name of a person whose innocence has been established can work to his great disadvantage as well. In this respect Bill C-213 could be regarded as inconsistent with its stated objective, namely, the furthering of the presumption of innocence.
Furthermore, Bill C-213 would preclude media disclosure of tactics which verge on harassment or vexatious proceedings such as multiple charges, multiple prosecutions, and unmeritorious appeals against acquittal.
Disclosure of misconduct by law enforcement personnel which is collateral to the commission of the offence charged could also be affected. In cases involving criminal misconduct of law enforcement personnel, and there are recent examples of that with regard to the detectives in the Lorenz case, for one, who forged affidavits, and also certain revelations by the McDonald commission, who are charged, plead guilty and obtain absolute discharges, the media would be precluded from identifying the culprits. This would have a deleterious effect on general and specific deterrence with a concomitant devastating impact on public confidence in the criminal justice system.
The difficulties of application or implementation are considerable. In the first place there is no reason why a convicted person should be protected from public view merely because he has received an absolute discharge. In addition, inequality in
the treatment of persons must necessarily arise. Consider the case of persons convicted of the same offence. Those who receive an absolute discharge get the benefit of prohibition, while persons sentenced to other nominal dispositions do not receive the same protection.
In relation to the application of the prohibition in cases where a person who is convicted receives a sentence-that is, other than an absolute discharge-publication would be permissible notwithstanding that that person consequently receives a pardon. Publication, having taken place before the pardon was granted, the intended purpose of Bill C-213 will be frustrated in at least this respect. On the other hand, why should the fact that a full pardon has been granted not be published, since publication may inure to the individual's benefit by vindicating him? Publication also ensures society's interests by guarding against unwarranted use of the power to pardon. For example, there is the newspaper coverage of a Newfoundland case and the Mississippi case where an outgoing governor sold pardons.
The prohibition, as drafted, would also extend to civil proceedings which arise out of the commission of an offence. In particular, proceedings for false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, defamation, assault and battery, etc. could be affected. How would law reports, law journals, bar association publications and so forth be affected by the blanket prohibition contained in Bill C-213? Would the minutes of convocation of law societies be prohibited from naming solicitors disbarred and charged after disciplinary proceedings? All of these questions are affected by the definition of newspaper in section 261 of the Criminal Code. In view of the outcomes enumerated above, it appears that Bill C-213 is inimical to its stated objectives, that is, the enhancement of the principle "innocent until proven guilty". Further, its destructive effect extends to harm other primary values of the criminal law.
Consider the question of the administrative feasibility of the proposal contained in the bill. It is not possible to give a precise answer to this question. However, it seems reasonable to assume that it will involve increased screening by the news media, with the result that enquiries to the courts should increase. There is likely to be an additional case load in view of the nature of the activity and scope of the prohibition.
Another matter to be considered is the compatibility of the bill with existing legislation and regulations, as well as its impact on present programs and mechanisms. The right to public trial is well established historically in both the common law and legislation. The Canadian Bill of Rights, section 1(f) provides for freedom of the press in Canada. It is likely that the media will regard this as an attempt to restrict this fundamental right. In addition section 2(f) of the Canadian Bill of Rights, which gives every person charged the right to a fair and public hearing, could be construed as enabling publication of the particulars sought to be prohibited.
On the other hand, a trial in public is not the same as a trial that may be reported in the newspaper. There already exists in
May 27, 1980

the Criminal Code provisions which either restrict absolutely any publication, such as section 441, and 141(2), or provide the court with the power in appropriate cases or circumstances to limit or preclude publication of all or part of the proceedings including the identity of witnesses and accused persons. I have mentioned sections 442, 457.2, 467, and 470. These provisions are directed toward the problem of newspaper or radio coverage of certain matters. Bill C-213 will, by implication, have the effect of limiting those sections of the Criminal Code which now give the court a discretion to prohibit newspaper publication or radio broadcast in so far as the name of an accused person is concerned.
It should also be noted in this context that the International Covenant on Human Rights, to which Canada is a signatory, Article 14(i), provides that:
1) All persons shall be equal before the courts and tribunals. In the determination of any criminal charge against him, or of his rights and obligations in a suit at law, everyone shall be entitled to a fair and public hearing by a competent, independent and impartial tribunal established by law. The press and the public may be excluded from all or part of a trial for reasons of morals, public order (ordre public) or national security in a democratic society, or when the interest of the private lives of the parties so requires, or to the extent strictly necessary in the opinion of the court in special circumstances where publicity would prejudice the interests of justice; but any judgment rendered in a criminal case or in a suit at law shall be made public except where the interest of juvenile persons otherwise requires or the proceedings concern matrimonial disputes or the guardianship of children.
Article 14(1), which embodies the principle that the press shall be admitted and be entitled to publish, recognizes specific exceptions to the principle of publicity which are founded on specific public interest and which are deemed to be of a higher order than the interests of publicity. Bill C-213 creates a blanket prohibition which could be regarded as restricting the application of this article. The mischief which Bill C-213 now seeks to redress is precluded by the present law of contempt of court.
Bill C-213 creates an offence of strict liability. The desirability of creating such an offence should be carefully considered in the light of the recommendations of the Law Reform Commission in their report "Our Criminal Law", which was to the contrary. Finally, in this context, it should also be noted that the Supreme Court of Canada will soon be considering an appeal involving the right of the public to all information relating to search warrants.
We must also consider the relationship that the proposal may have to any planned legislative programs of the Department of Justice. In the ongoing review of criminal law the Department of Justice has identified all aspects of the issue of pre-trial procedures, including publicity and the law of contempt of court, for review in conjunction with the Law Reform Commission as part of its criminal law reform program.
In the circumstances and for the reasons outlined, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) considers the passage of this proposed legislation inappropriate at this time.

We are told that over the next 50 years pensions will be in for increased buffeting. Six people today working support one pensioner, and within 50 years there will be three people working to support that same pensioner. That is a very serious matter. Ten years after that, if he is lucky to live to 85, or unlucky, the dollar will be worth only ten cents.

If one looks at the Canada Pension Plan one will find that there is a limit in that plan in terms of the yearly average insurable earnings of something like $13,000. I know of certain members of Parliament who make a little more than twice that, not to mention a number of other people in society, and who pay 1.8 per cent of $13,000. Actually I am told that it is a little less than $13,000 because of some sort of formula that is applied.
But if the 1.8 per cent were applied to the full earnings, instead of a limit of $13,000 on the yearly average earnings, it would change things quite a bit. It would provide more money for CPP funding which would provide the pensioner with a portable contributory plan, a higher income, and the Canada Pension Plan would no longer be considered a supplementary plan worth approximately 25 per cent. If people do not have a contributory plan to support them when they retire, then they call upon the non-contributory, except through taxation, plans of the kind we are speaking of tonight.
What this country needs is a plan that will be portable, adequate, contributory, and available to all, including housewives, because they are among the most vulnerable. My colleagues have stated that we in the NDP will support Bill C-16. A $35 increase for senior citizens is an important start, but it is not enough. In particular, Bill C-16 does not cover the increasing costs of shelter, fuel, utilities, and home repairs-essential costs that I am sure you realize are escalating almost every day. Pensioners with no other income will still be far below the poverty line. We in the NDP advocated a $40 increase per month for all elderly people on basic pensions, not just those on the guaranteed income supplement. This, along with a shelter grant, could bring income of pensioners closer to the poverty line.
Ideally, of course, we should have an adequate guaranteed income, not guaranteed poverty, with cost of living increases on a regular basis. This should be available to eliminate poverty for Canadians of all ages, not only for senior citizens.
Tonight I want to focus briefly on the high cost of shelter which is a major expense for senior citizens, particularly for those who are having to rent accommodations at market prices. I hope the minister will take particular note of this and will include this in future planning if not in this bill. Shelter costs are a major concern of senior citizens, depending, of
course, on where a person lives. Almost every senior citizen, regardless of income, has a major problem with accommodation and housing costs today.
First are those persons lucky enough to have had a home during their lifetime, a home that is paid for. Second, we have many senior citizens who are also very lucky to live in senior citizens housing developments, non-profit housing, where they pay 25 per cent of their income for shelter. Then we have the hidden pensioners who have great problems. I suspect many of them are the parents of members sitting in this House tonight who live in nice middle-class apartments, have had comfortable professional backgrounds perhaps, and yet are also paying exorbitant rents probably out of very limited pensions. It is known through research that of the many people in Canada who pay 50 per cent to 60 per cent of their incomes on rent- and this is many thousands of people-most of these are senior citizens and women. And 50 per cent to 60 per cent of senior citizens pensions is certainly something which is a very drastic cost.
Finally are the group of people, many of whom I am familiar with in my own riding who live in downtown flophouses or unsafe fire trap rooming houses, or in damp, cold basements and who are living on welfare, in some cases living on less.
First of all, dealing with the home owners, we know there are many pensioners who own their own homes and who may seem to have many advantages. However, with the increasingly high cost of fuel, home repairs, taxes and utilities, this is not necessarily so. Home owners with no extra income find it difficult to meet increasing costs. Often they are overhoused with homes too large for them, as families have grown up and moved away and they have little choice to move elsewhere.
These are the people who ideally, if more RRAP funds were available, could afford perhaps to subdivide and house other people. They are also finding that their houses and the repairs that go with them are an increasing burden. Too often these seniors in their own homes are more isolated than those in housing developments, without families around and who are somewhat isolated from their neighbours. The New Democratic Party during the recent election proposed a grant for elderly home owners that would help them pay their increased taxes. It was not much. It was $120 a year, but we would urge that this is justified for many of our seniors who are trapped in the high cost of owning their own homes.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The borrowing authority bill now before the House seeks borrowing authority of $12 billion for the fiscal year 1980-81. This bill also seeks explicit authorization for the government to borrow in foreign currencies as well as in Canadian dollars.
As hon. members will recall, on April 21 last I tabled in the House of Commons a projection of the government's budgetary and non-budgetary cash requirements for fiscal year 198081.1 indicated at that time that that statement was a necessary foundation for a request which I would be making later for a borrowing authority. The requirements forecast in that projection amount to $11,730 million. This amount excludes requirements for foreign exchange transactions.
In addition to these forecast cash requirements, there is always the need for a substantial margin of borrowing authority to provide for contingencies. For example, there are major uncertainties arising from foreign exchange transactions since either a major weakening or a major strengthening of the exchange rate would have an impact upon the borrowing requirements of the government. If the Canadian dollar were to be strong, then the government would have to raise more Canadian dollars to borrow foreign exchange. On the other hand, the Canadian dollar could be or might be weak. Under those circumstances the government would then be faced with the need to borrow foreign currencies.
This margin of borrowing authority is being provided by unused borrowing authority obtained prior to November, 1979, and which is not subject to automatic cancellation at the end of the fiscal year. I believe that when the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) made a similar request last November in the House, he referred to this unused borrowing authority which had not expired and which indeed has not expired up to the present time.
This borrowing authority was obtained prior to November, 1979, and was not subject to automatic cancellation at the end of the fiscal year. This unused borrowing authority which is
available for use at any time and which has been carried forward, amounted to approximately $2.9 billion at the beginning of fiscal year 1980-81. All unused borrowing authority obtained under the Borrowing Authority Act 1979-80 was cancelled or lapsed on March 31, 1980. As I recollect, that refers to the borrowing authority which was granted by the House at the request of the former minister of finance. Consequently to date in fiscal 1980-81 new moneys raised have been charged to the $2.9 billion of unused borrowing authority obtained earlier and carried forward. However, these unused borrowing powers are rapidly being used up and the government requires new borrowing authority to enable it to continue with the 1980-81 debt program.
The borrowing authority of $12 billion now being requested, along with the remaining portion of the unused borrowing powers obtained in prior years and still available, should be sufficient to complete the borrowing program this fiscal year as well as to provide a margin for contingencies.
All outstanding and unused borrowing authority provided by this new act for fiscal 1980-81 in respect of which no action has been taken by the governor in council, pursuant to section 37 of the Financial Administration Act, will be cancelled on March 31, 1981.
Hon. members will recognize that, referring to clause (2) of the bill, we seek certain clarification with respect to borrowing in foreign currencies. Over the years the government has borrowed in many currencies including U.S. dollars, British pounds, Deutschmarks and lira, and has always honoured its debts in the currency of contract. This clause, the one to which I referred, will serve to confirm the authority of the government to borrow and repay loans in currencies other than Canadian dollars.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very signal occasion in the history of this session of Parliament because we have actually had the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) speak. This is his second speech. The House opened on April 14 and this is the second time the minister has spoken. The last time he spoke was on the occasion of his bootlegged mini-budget that he introduced toward the end of April.
This is a very short statement. We are expecting a bit more from the minister. We hope that when he speaks to close the debate he will actually tell us something. It is his history in this House to speak but never to say anything. Before I am through with the few remarks I am going to be making on this bill, which are always succinct and to the point, I will analyse and dissect some of the answers the minister has given to questions in this House on various serious issues of economic and financial approaches by the government.
The minister has said, and he can hardly deny it since it is in the bill, that the bill is to authorize the government to borrow some $12 billion during this financial year. It is to give the government borrowing authority for $12 billion. I recall that in the bill I brought into the House last fall on October 23, we were asking the House to authorize us to borrow $7 billion.
May 27, 1980

Some Liberal members, probably risking being kicked out of the caucus then said, "That's terrible. You have lost control." That is what they said when we brought in the bill to authorize the borrowing of $7 billion.
The hon. gentleman who is practically a deskmate of the Minister of Finance, that tattle-tale "Gray" Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), said we should only have $3.5 billion. He said we did not need $7 billion. He made a rough calculation and he came up with $3.5 billion. I am going to make a rough calculation tonight and say that $6 billion is more than enough for the hon. gentleman until he produces some facts and figures to show why he needs the $12 billion. In other words, when is he going to bring in his budget? Why is he such a reluctant virgin in a financial sense? He doesn't want to bring a budget into this House. He doesn't want to show the Canadian people and the business community what his financial plans are, what his economic policies are going to be. Why is he so reluctant to do this when he and his minions back last October and November were urging that a budget be brought in very rapidly? I will refer later to the remarks which were made by them last fall.
The minister says he has a margin. He says there was unused borrowing authority of $2.9 billion at the beginning of the 1980-81 fiscal year. That's at the beginning of that year, April 1, 1980. So the minister had unused borrowing authority of $2.9 billion at that time, he said. But he did not tell us how much of that is unused tonight. Are we not, as members of Parliament, entitled to know, when the minister comes by looking for a mere $12 billion in borrowing authority, just what is left of the $2.9 billion he had on April 1 ? Why is he so reluctant to give members of the House and the people of Canada that information? Why does he make this short little spavined excuse of a speech when he introduced this bill, neglecting even to tell us how much is left of the old $2.9 billion that he had a few short weeks ago?
This spendthrift minister, this spender-he and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) are helpless in the hands of his colleagues. But before this bill passes the House we want to know how much of the unused borrowing authority is left of the $2.9 billion the minister says he had on April 1. This is being rapidly used up, he says. You are darned right it's being rapidly used up because the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is a man who says he does not worry about the deficit. So it is certainly being used up rapidly. But we would like to know how rapidly. We ask the minister to let us in on the secret. After all, he is asking for $12 billion.
In addition, the minister neglects to tell the House that he has borrowing authority for every billion dollars he repays in debt coming due. For every $100 million in Canada Savings Bonds people want to redeem, the minister has the right to borrow another $100 million. Or another billion dollars. So how much unused authority does he have in those directions- or is that included in the $2.9 billion? The minister is a silent minister. He reminds me of something people used to have in
Borrowing Authority Act
their homes at one time-the silent butler. This is the silent minister, the Sysco Kid. He is in a constant soft-shoe dance. He is a soft-shoe dancer without parallel in the world. Never have we seen such an example of soft-shoe dancing as this minister tiptoeing through the question period. And now he wants authority to borrow $12 billion to help the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. MacLaren) who has a $3.1 billion oil import compensation bill to meet-
At a minimum.

-at a minimum. Or is it $4 billion, or is it $5 billion? And the House is being asked to authorize $12 billion for this profligate minister, this silent minister, this demure minister, this shy minister, this reluctant minister-
Hear, hear!

Tell us how much of that is for the oil import compensation program. Perhaps the people of Canada are interested. Perhaps they are not. I don't know. This is the minister who refuses to have the House of Commons finance committee look into the question of the interest rates. The same group of people who last fall were so anxious to examine interest rates no longer want Parliament to look into the interest rate question at all. Has the minister had a quick change in his thinking?
You just don't show up, John!

I am getting ready for the business of the House here. Mr. Speaker, have you ever heard the carrion crow? We are certainly hearing a lot of crowing and cawing tonight. Just listen. The House of Commons opened on April 14, 43 days ago. This government took office on March 3, 85 days ago-it seems like 85 years-and there has not been a single initiative in the financial area or the economic area to help the people of Canada in all that time, not one, except for the bill which went through the House tonight, the one the Liberals and the NDP filibustered to stop it going through, the $35 additional assistance to old age pensioners. It was filibustered by the Liberal and NDP members.
Mr. Speaker, there have been only two issues in which this government has been interested-Quebec and patronage. This is all they have had on their minds in those 85 days. Only two issues have they faced-the Quebec separatist issue and patronage, and we don't know which comes first. Both are very much on their minds. This is a guano government which believes in fouling its own nest. That is what it is doing. I asked a question in the House yesterday. I asked how much of this money is going to be used in connection with the refusal of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to put the water transport assistance directorate down in St. John's, Newfoundland, where it was promised it would go on February 16, 1979. How much is being spent on that, and the counteraction of that move, if it is to be counteracted?
How much of the money borrowed will be spent on the Port Hope finagle, the movement of the uranium refinery from Port

May 27, 1980
Adjournment Debate
Hope to Northern Ontario? How much will be spent on stopping the move of the regional forestry office from Cornwall to Peterborough? How much is to go to Charlottetown in additional expenses caused by the interference of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) in the location of the site of the DVA building down in Charlottetown? A shameful record of patronage.
Mr. Speaker, one out of every four of the tax dollars paid by the Canadian people this year will go toward payment of interest as a result of the honourable spendthrifts opposite, with the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), the Sysco Kid, leading the ranks. How much of this borrowed money will go to the Sysco plant? When will the minister follow up on his commitment to the Sysco plant down in Cape Breton?
Our position is this: five months ago, practically six months ago, our government was defeated because of the budget which I presented to the House.
The people didn't want you any more!
Oh, oh!

Honourable howling monkeys opposite. They are either monkeys or donkeys. Even with the majority they have, they are afraid to listen in case I might induce some of them to cross the floor. Almost six months ago, hon. gentlemen opposite defeated the budget we put forward outlining our plans for dealing with the economic problems facing the country. Why are they now so reluctant, having defeated our proposals, to come forward with their own? They were so ready to defeat us on December 13 that they called members in from the hospitals with their ruptures, their hernias, and everything else. They risked the lives of those people to defeat the government. They are afraid, now, to bring in a budget of their own. When do they propose to tell the people how they intend to deal with the problems facing the economy?
What about the 6,000 miners up in Labrador city and Wabush who have just been advised they will be laid off in the month of July because of the reduction in iron ore sales to the United States, the immediate effects upon Canada of the U.S. recession? Why doesn't the minister bring in a budget telling us what he intends to do, or not do, about this recession?
May I call it ten o'clock, Monsieur Speaker?
Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, my question on the late show this evening has to do with two questions, really. One was posed on May 1, as reported at page 600 of Hansard, by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney) to the minister responsible for fitness and amateur sport, and the other was my question on May 26 of this year as reported at page 1392 of Hansard. I believe the minister responsible for fitness and amateur sport, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan), or whatever his title is, is just not quite sure of what is going on in the lottery field. In view of the new face on federalism the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is now trying to portray to Canada, I am sure the Prime Minister would like his ministers to recognize that such jurisdictional questions as resource taxation, offshore mineral rights, federal spending power, federal trade and commerce power, communications and lotteries are as important and valid as patriation of the constitution.
How can the Prime Minister allow a minister-a former premier-to break an agreement with the provinces which was duly signed by the federal and provincial ministers, his conter-parts, and scrutinized under the guidance of the Privy Council Office and by the Department of Justice? How can he expect any provincial government to believe him in the future?
That is what you did.

The provincial governments have now accumulated $170,000 in interest, and I doubt whether the federal government will ever receive that money. I realize that the former premier does not think the amount is much. After all, his salary and perhaps a few additional trust funds make that look like peanuts.
Come on, that is not like you, Steve.

However, Your Honour, athletes, ballets, symphonies, the Stratford Theatre and small theatres can use that money, and they can use it right now. The agreement was made by the ten provinces. The cheque was paid one day ahead of time. It was due on March 31. It was accepted by the executive assistant of the Minister of Labour, sent back on April 14, and the cheque was approximately $6,150,000. The next cheque will be due on June 30. I wonder whether that will be sent back.
1 want just to bring this House up to date on the agreement because I think this minister is really not aware of what has happened. I do not like to talk about former ministers who are not in the House any more. My predecessor was a good minister; nevertheless, she did not have an agreement, and I would just like to express this to the House.
On January 14, 1980, as minister of state for fitness and amateur sport I announced that the cabinet had approved the equal splitting of lottery revenues for arts and culture and fitness and amateur sport by endorsing the terms of the recent federal-provincial agreement on the transfer of Loto Canada to the provinces.
May 27, 1980

The cabinet had agreed that the $24 million guaranteed annually from the provinces, and indexed from 1979 to the cost of living, would be shared equally, with $12 million being directed to amateur sport, fitness and physical recreation programs, and $12 million to arts and culture programs.
The $24 million annual Loto revenues would have been over and above the funds voted by Parliament, that is, incremental to the budget.
I was most pleased to provide Canadians with an example of the practical benefits which do result from a co-operative approach to federal-provincial relations. The provinces had gained new funding. The public would have seen less of its lottery dollar eaten away by duplicate advertising and administrative costs, and the federal government had a source of revenue totally secure against both inflation and government spending cuts to devote to the cultural and physical well being of our citizens.
By dedicating the funds to these two areas the federal government was demonstrating its commitment and increased support to two very important areas. During the previous four years Loto Canada had only provided an average of $2.5 million per year to fitness and amateur sport.
I would like to read the agreement. This was sent to all ministers, but perhaps the minister does not have a copy of it, so I should put it into Hansard.
My Dear Minister:
On behalf of the Government of Canada, we are pleased to confirm the agreement reached at the August 21 meeting in Ottawa, the principal terms of which are as follows:
(1)	The Government of Canada, through its agent Loto Canada Inc., will withdraw from the sale of lottery tickets, effective December 31, 1979.
(2)	The Government of Canada will cause Loto Canada Inc. to be wound up after December 31, 1979, under the Canada Business Corporations Act, as quickly as legal, financial and administrative requirements permit.
(3)	On and after January 1, 1980, the provinces will jointly remit annually to the Government of Canada the sum of $24 million payable in quarterly instalments of $6 million and adjustments, commencing April 1, 1980. The provinces shall agree-
I should like to emphasize that this was in 1979 dollars connected with the CPI. It continues:
-among themselves as to the proportion to be paid by each province.
Each quarterly instalment shall be adjusted as to reflect the effects of inflation, utilizing the consumer price index as the standard of measurement and 1979 as the base year.
This was signed by the then minister of state for fitness and amateur sport, the hon. member for Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski); the Hon. David MacDonald who was then secretary of state; the then minister of state for federal-provincial relations, the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis). Also it was signed by ministers for the provinces of Alberta, Nova Scotia, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island, Manitoba, Ontario, New Brunswick, Quebec, Saskatchewan and Newfoundland. It was completely signed, sealed and delivered.

Mr. Speaker, I can assure my colleague opposite that the minister responsible for physical fitness and amateur sport indeed will hear what he had to say in the House tonight.
I might mention that I am slightly disappointed in that the hon. member mentioned things which of course were extraneous to the matter before us. There are a few things I should like to point out.
First of all, there is some question as to the legal validity of the August, 1979, letter agreement between the provinces and the former Progressive Conservative government that led to the federal withdrawal from the lottery business. Parts of the letter agreement are vague and incomplete. It cannot be considered the necessary formal federal-provincial agreement in that an order in council concerning the matter was never even issued.
Furthermore, the decision to terminate the operations of Loto Canada was shortsighted in that it would significantly limit the federal government's ability to contribute financially toward fitness, amateur sports, arts and culture. Also, it would seriously curtail federal funding of major national events and programs in the culture and sports areas. The hon. member was so proud when he said that we were going to get $24 million a year. Let it be known that the net annual profits of Loto Canada were in the area of $76 million. This member opposite was the minister for sport at the time. He should

May 27, 1980

know that the former Progressive Conservative government agreed to withdraw from the business in return for annual payments from the provinces of only $24 million.
Shame!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Sports)

Big deal. We are so willing to give away our money at the federal level where we can carry on national programs, and all for what? Is it so that we can bow again before the provinces?
